    Unit 1.1

    Flowering and non-flowering plants

    Theory

    1Two big plant families

    Every plant needs to reproduce — to make new plants like itself. HOW they do it splits plants into two big families: flowering plants use flowers to make seeds — like mango, rice and sunflowers. Non-flowering plants never grow a flower — they use spores (ferns, moss) or cones (pine trees).

    2Flowering plants: the flower is a seed factory

    In a flowering plant, the flower is the reproduction factory. After the flower is pollinated it wilts, and its base swells into a fruit holding seeds. Each seed carries a baby plant. So: wherever you see a fruit or a seed, there was once a flower! This family is the biggest — about 352,000 species, from tiny grasses to giant mango trees.

    Flower → Fruit → SeedMango, orange, rice, beans — every one began as a flower.
    Careful: not every flower is showy!Grass and rice flowers are tiny and pale green — but they are real flowers.

    3Non-flowering plants: spores and cones

    Ferns and moss reproduce with spores — dust-like specks packed in little brown dots under a fern's leaf, so light the wind carries them everywhere. Conifers like pines and firs hide their seeds inside woody cones instead: when the cone dries and opens its scales, winged seeds spin out. Neither group ever needs a flower!

    4How to classify like a scientist

    Met a mystery plant? Ask like a botanist: (1) Does it have flowers — even tiny green ones? (2) Does it have fruit or seeds? (Fruit → there must have been a flower.) (3) Can you find cones or spore dots? One clue — a flower, a fruit, or bare seeds in a cone — and you can classify it. Don't be fooled by size — a small grass has flowers, a giant pine does not!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna finds 4 plants: a mango tree, a fern, a pine tree and a rice plant. Sort them into flowering / non-flowering.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Mango makes fruit → it must have flowers.
    2. Rice has tiny pale-green flowers → flowering.
    3. The fern carries spores and the pine carries cones → non-flowering.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: flowering — mango and rice; non-flowering — fern (spores) and pine (cones).
    Example 2

    Nyna's friend says: “A pine tree has no flowers, so it can't have seeds.” Is that right?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Flowers are only ONE way to make seeds.
    2. Conifers make seeds inside woody cones.
    3. No flowers ≠ no seeds!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: wrong — a pine has no flowers but still makes seeds, hidden in its cones. Only ferns and mosses use spores instead of seeds.
    Example 3

    The damp wall behind the house wears a soft green “carpet” that never flowers. What is it, and how does it reproduce?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. A soft, low green mat loving damp shade — the signature of moss.
    2. Moss belongs to the non-flowering family.
    3. It spreads by dust-light spores.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: it's moss — a non-flowering plant that reproduces and spreads by wind-blown spores.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The life cycle is a loop

    A flowering plant's life cycle is not a straight line — it is a LOOP that repeats forever: seed → germination → seedling → mature plant → flower → fruit with seeds → new seed. Each new seed starts the loop again. That is how one mango tree can become a whole orchard!

    2From seed to seedling

    The cycle opens with germination: the seed drinks water, swells, and cracks its coat. The root always grows DOWN first — anchoring the plant and finding water. Then the shoot climbs UP towards light. When the first true leaves unfold, we have a seedling — from now on it cooks its own food using sunlight.

    The order is always: root first, shoot secondWater and anchoring come first; light comes second.
    A seedling cannot flower yetIt must become a mature plant first — weeks for some species, 40 years for an oak!

    3Maturing, flowering, fruiting

    Once big enough, the mature plant pours its energy into flowering. A pollinated flower then wilts — its petals drop because their job is done — and the flower's base swells into a fruit hugging the seeds. The fruit ripens, the seeds travel, and in fresh soil somewhere… the cycle begins all over again.

    4Fast loops and slow loops

    Not every loop runs at the same speed! Rice sprints through its whole cycle in ~4 months — farmers grow 2–3 crops a year. A sunflower needs ~1 season. An oak strolls: 40 YEARS before its first acorn. Fast or slow, the stages always follow the same order: seed, seedling, mature plant, flower, fruit.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Put these stages in the right order: flower — seed — mature plant — seedling — fruit.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Everything starts with the seed.
    2. The seed germinates into a seedling, which grows into a mature plant.
    3. The mature plant flowers; the pollinated flower becomes fruit holding new seeds.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: seed → seedling → mature plant → flower → fruit (then the seeds inside the fruit start the loop again).
    Example 2

    Nyna plants a bean in a jar. On day 3, a “white thread” pokes out and grows DOWNWARD. Is it the root or the shoot? Why downward?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which part always appears FIRST in germination?
    2. What is its job — finding light, or finding water?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: it is the root — the first part to emerge. It grows down to anchor the plant and find water; the shoot comes later, climbing up towards the light.
    Example 3

    Nyna's rose flower has just wilted and dropped its petals. Mum wants to throw the plant away, thinking it has died. Has it?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. In the life cycle, what happens RIGHT AFTER a flower wilts?
    2. Petals drop because their job is done — what job?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: no! Wilting is a normal life-cycle stage — after pollination the petals drop and the flower's base swells into a fruit with seeds. The plant is alive and well.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Inside a flower

    A flower is a clever machine. Showy petals are the advertising posters. The stamen — the MALE part — carries an anther on top, dusted with yellow pollen. The carpel — the FEMALE part — has a sticky stigma up top and an ovary with egg cells below. And at the flower's base wait drops of sweet nectar.

    2Pollination: the pollen delivery

    ​Pollination = pollen leaving one flower's ANTHER and landing on another flower's STIGMA (same species). The courier? A pollinator — a bee drops in for nectar, gets dusted with pollen, then accidentally delivers it at the next flower. Then comes fertilisation: pollen joins an egg in the ovary — and a seed begins to form.

    Pollination = the deliveryPollen travels anther (male) → sticky stigma (female).
    Fertilisation = after deliveryPollen meets egg in the ovary → a seed starts. Two different steps!

    3Who delivers? Animals and the wind

    Flowers hire two kinds of couriers. Animals (bees, butterflies, birds, bats): the flower pays in nectar and advertises with bright petals and scent. Wind (grass, rice, corn): no adverts needed — flowers are small, pale, nectar-free, but release HUGE clouds of light pollen for the wind to carry. Look at a flower and you can guess its courier!

    4Why pollination matters to US

    No pollination → no fertilisation → no seeds → NO FRUIT. Mangoes, watermelons, apples, tomatoes, chocolate (from cacao flowers!) — all depend on pollinators. That is why scientists worry when bee numbers fall, and why many fruit farmers keep beehives right in their orchards. Protecting pollinators = protecting our own dinner.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A bee lands on flower A, gets dusted with pollen, then flies to flower B of the same species. Name the part where the pollen STARTED on flower A and where it LANDS on flower B.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Pollen is MADE on the male part — the tip of the stamen.
    2. Pollen must STICK on the female part — the sticky tip of the carpel.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: it starts on flower A's anther — and lands on flower B's stigma.
    Example 2

    Rice flowers are tiny, pale green, scentless and nectar-free. Which courier do they use for pollination? How do you know?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. No adverts (bright petals), no payment (nectar) → not aimed at animals.
    2. What is the only free courier left?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the wind. Wind-pollinated flowers don't need beauty or scent — they just release lots of light pollen into the air.
    Example 3

    A sealed greenhouse grows cucumbers — no bees can get in. Flowers bloom everywhere, but no fruit appears. What should the farmer do?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. No bees → pollen never delivered → no fertilisation → no fruit.
    2. Someone must do the bee's job instead…
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: hand-pollinate — use a small brush to move pollen from one flower's anther to another's stigma (or release a hive of bees inside). Real farmers do exactly this!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Why must seeds leave home?

    If every seed dropped right under its parent, the seedlings would COMPETE with the parent and each other — for the same light, the same water, the same patch of soil. Dispersal solves this: send the seeds FAR AWAY, to places with light, water and space of their own. Plants cannot walk — so their seeds must be the travellers!

    Far from home = less competitionLight, water and empty soil all to the seedling's self.
    Dropped in place = crowdedSeedlings starve in their own parent's shadow.

    2The seed's four travel companies

    ​WIND: light seeds with silky parachutes (dandelion) or spinning wings (maple). WATER: seeds that float — coconuts cross oceans. ANIMALS: two tricks — hooked burrs hitch rides on fur, or sweet fruit gets eaten and the seeds get "planted" in droppings with free fertiliser. SELF-EXPLOSION: drying pods twist and explode, flinging seeds away.

    3A seed's shape tells its travel story

    A scientist can read a seed's ticket from its shape. Light + fluffy/winged → WIND. Waterproof + buoyant → WATER (a coconut's husk is a built-in life jacket). Hooked → ANIMAL FUR. Wrapped in sweet, bright fruit → ANIMAL STOMACH. A drying, twisting pod → about to POP! Every feature is an evolved tool serving one goal: travel far.

    4Dispersal ≠ pollination — don't mix them up!

    Two different journeys in the life cycle: pollination moves POLLEN between FLOWERS — so seeds can be made (unit 1.3). Dispersal moves finished SEEDS away — so seedlings find new homes. A bee carrying pollen = pollination. A bird eating fruit and carrying seeds = dispersal. To tell them apart, ask: is the traveller pollen, or a seed?

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna finds 3 seeds: (a) one with a fluffy white tuft, (b) one inside a sweet red berry, (c) one covered in prickly hooks. Work out how each travels.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Fluff = a parachute → what does it ride?
    2. Sweet fruit = an invitation to eat → where do the seeds travel?
    3. Hooks grip whatever brushes past — what would that be?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) wind — the silky parachute drifts on the breeze; (b) fruit-eating animals — seeds get "planted" in droppings far away; (c) animal fur — the burr hitch-hikes on passing coats.
    Example 2

    Why do coconut palms grow along tropical beaches all over the world — even on islands thousands of kilometres from the mainland?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. A coconut falls into the sea — does it sink or float?
    2. What are the fibrous husk and waterproof shell for?
    3. Where do the currents take it?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: coconuts disperse by WATER. The air-filled husk works as a life jacket and the waterproof shell protects the seed for months at sea; ocean currents deliver it to distant sands — and a new palm sprouts right at the waterline.
    Example 3

    On a hot afternoon, Nyna hears tiny “snap! snap!” sounds from the bean bushes — and sees beans landing a metre away from the plants. What is happening?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What does hot sun do to the bean pods?
    2. The drying pod shrinks and twists — until what happens?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: EXPLOSION dispersal. The sun dries the pods, which twist like winding springs; at the breaking point they snap open and catapult the seeds away — the plant is its own seed launcher!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Inside a seed

    A seed is a three-part survival kit: the embryo — a tiny sleeping baby plant; the food store — a packed lunch for the first days; and the seed coat — armour against drying out and knocks. With this kit a seed can wait months, years — even thousands of years — for the right moment.

    2The three keys that wake a seed

    A seed only germinates when THREE keys turn together: WATER — the seed drinks, swells and cracks its coat; WARMTH — the signal that winter is over; OXYGEN — the seed must "breathe" to burn its food store for energy. One key missing, and the seed sleeps on. Note: LIGHT is not needed yet — it is pitch dark underground and seeds sprout anyway!

    Needed: water + warmth + oxygenAll three at once — like the three keys of a safe.
    Not needed yet: light and soilThe food store replaces light; wet cotton can replace soil. Both matter only AFTER the shoot surfaces.

    3The germination sequence

    The sequence never changes: (1) the seed drinks and swells; (2) the coat cracks; (3) the ROOT emerges first, digging down — anchor and water; (4) the SHOOT pushes up through the soil towards light; (5) the first leaves unfold — now the plant cooks its own food with sunlight, just as the seed's lunch box runs empty. A perfectly timed relay race!

    4Fair tests with seeds

    Want to prove seeds need water? Run a fair test: two identical jars, same seeds, same temperature, same air — only ONE thing different: jar A gets water, jar B stays dry. If only jar A sprouts, you have proven water's role! Change just one condition at a time — that is how scientists isolate each "key".

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna puts bean seeds in 3 jars: (1) damp cotton, warm kitchen; (2) damp cotton, fridge; (3) dry cotton, warm kitchen. After a week, which jar has sprouts? Why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Check each jar against the 3 keys: water? warmth? oxygen?
    2. What is jar 2 missing? What about jar 3?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: only jar 1 sprouts — it has water + warmth + air. Jar 2 has water but is too cold; jar 3 is warm but dry. One missing key, and the seed keeps sleeping.
    Example 2

    A seed germinates in pitch-dark soil with no sunlight at all. Where does it get the energy to grow?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Recall the seed's three-part survival kit.
    2. Which part is the packed lunch?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: from the food store inside the seed. The seed "burns" this store (needing oxygen!) to grow its root and shoot. Sunlight is only needed once leaves reach the surface and start making food.
    Example 3

    Why do seeds of cold-country plants usually NOT germinate in the mild autumn, but wait through winter and sprout in spring?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What would await a tender seedling that sprouted in November?
    2. What does the waiting protect the seed from?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: sprouting in autumn is a death sentence — frost would kill the seedling. Many seeds are "programmed" to need a long cold spell before waking with warmth: guaranteeing they rise in early spring, with a whole warm season ahead.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Every sound is a vibration

    Sound's big secret: every sound is made by something VIBRATING. A vibration is a super-fast back-and-forth movement. Hit a drum — the skin vibrates. Pluck a guitar string — it blurs with vibration. Speak — the vocal cords in your throat vibrate. The vibrating object is the sound's source. Stop the vibration, and the sound stops — instantly!

    2Sound needs a medium to travel

    Vibrations do not fly to your ear on their own — they must pass THROUGH a material: a medium. The vibrating source bumps nearby air particles, which bump the next ones… like a row of dominoes, forming a sound wave. Air, water, wood and metal all carry sound — solids even carry it BETTER than air! But in a vacuum like outer space: no particles to bump → total silence.

    A medium → sound travelsAir ~340 m/s · water ~1,500 m/s · steel faster still.
    A vacuum → silenceMovie explosions booming in space? Science says: impossible!

    3How your ear hears

    A drumbeat's journey: drum skin vibrates → sound waves race through air → your outer ear catches them like a funnel → the waves make your eardrum — a thin skin stretched like a tiny drum — VIBRATE along → tiny bones amplify the wiggle → nerve signals fly to the brain → you "hear"! In other words: your ear is a vibration catcher.

    4Seeing and feeling vibrations

    Vibrations are usually too fast to see — but you can catch them red-handed: sprinkle rice on a drum and tap — the rice JUMPS! Pluck a rubber band — it blurs. Hum with a hand on your throat — it tickles. Touch a speaker — feel the beat. And the reverse trick: to STOP a sound, STOP the vibration — pinch the rubber band, grab the ringing bell. Vibration ends, sound ends — perfect proof!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna sprinkles rice on a drum. When she taps the drum, the rice bounces. When she presses her whole hand on the drum skin, the sound stops at once. Explain both.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The rice bounces because the drum skin is doing what?
    2. The pressing hand stops the skin from doing what?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the rice bounces because the skin is VIBRATING — the vibration flicks it upward. The pressed hand STOPS the vibration; no vibration, no sound. Proof that sound = vibration.
    Example 2

    Two divers underwater can clearly hear a motorboat. But two astronauts standing next to each other in space cannot hear each other at all, even shouting. Why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Is water a sound medium?
    2. Between the astronauts, is there any material to vibrate?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: water is an excellent medium (about 4× faster than air), so the divers hear clearly. Space is a vacuum — no particles to pass the vibration along, so no shout can cross from one astronaut to the other. (That's what radios are for!)
    Example 3

    Long ago, people pressed an ear to the railway track to detect a distant train before hearing anything through the air. How does this trick work?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The steel rail is a solid.
    2. Do solids carry sound faster or slower than air?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: steel carries sound much faster and farther than air. The train's wheel vibrations race kilometres along the rail to the pressed ear — while the airborne sound hasn't arrived yet. Solids are sound's highway!

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is volume?

    ​Volume tells us whether a sound is loud or quiet. The secret is the SIZE of the vibration, called its amplitude: hit a drum HARD → the skin swings further → big amplitude → loud sound. Tap it GENTLY → tiny wiggle → quiet sound. Same drum, same note — only the size of the vibration changes!

    2Measuring volume in decibels

    Scientists measure volume in decibels (dB), using a sound meter. A reference ladder: rustling leaves ~20 dB · a whisper ~20–30 dB · conversation ~60 dB · busy traffic ~85 dB · a chainsaw ~110 dB · close thunder ~120 dB. Watch out: the dB scale climbs FAST — every +10 dB means about 10× more sound energy!

    385 dB — the hearing safety line

    Your ears are amazing — and fragile. Long exposure to sounds above 85 dB slowly damages your hearing — and this damage does NOT heal. That is why builders wear ear defenders, airport crews wear protectors, and your headphones belong below half volume. Too much noise is not just annoying — it is a real health hazard.

    Below 85 dB: safeConversation, moderate music, classrooms — comfortable all day.
    Above 85 dB: limit your time!The louder it is, the shorter the safe time — and 120 dB+ can hurt instantly.

    4Volume fades with distance

    The farther you stand from a source, the quieter it sounds. Why? Sound waves spread out in all directions like an inflating ball — the energy gets stretched over a bigger and bigger area. Beside a festival speaker: deafening. Two streets away: background hum. That is why sound meters always note the DISTANCE of the measurement!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Order these sounds from QUIETEST to LOUDEST: busy traffic, rustling leaves, close thunder, normal conversation.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Assign decibels: leaves ~20, conversation ~60, traffic ~85, thunder ~120.
    2. Sort in increasing order.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: rustling leaves (20 dB) → conversation (60 dB) → traffic (85 dB) → close thunder (120 dB).
    Example 2

    Two sound waves have the same number of ripples, but wave B is three times TALLER than wave A. Which sound is louder, and which quantity tells you?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What is the scientific name for a wave's height?
    2. What does a bigger amplitude mean for your ears?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: wave B is louder. A wave's height is its AMPLITUDE — bigger amplitude means a stronger vibration carrying more energy, heard as a louder sound.
    Example 3

    Nyna's uncle works on a building site where the drill measures 100 dB. Does he need ear protection? Use the safety line to answer.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Where does the hearing safety line sit, in dB?
    2. Which side of the line is 100 dB — and he works there ALL DAY.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: absolutely yes! 100 dB is well above the 85 dB line, and all-day exposure would permanently damage his hearing. Ear defenders cut the volume reaching his ears to a safe level.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Pitch: high sounds and low sounds

    ​Pitch tells us whether a sound is high or low. The secret is the SPEED of the vibration: fast vibrations → high sounds, like birdsong or a mouse's squeak. Slow vibrations → low sounds, like a big drum or thunder's rumble. Careful: pitch is NOT volume — a mosquito's whine is quiet AND high; a lion's roar is loud AND low!

    2Frequency and hertz

    Scientists measure pitch as frequency — VIBRATIONS PER SECOND — in hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 vibration per second. The orchestra's tuning note A = 440 Hz (the string wiggles 440 times a second!). Human ears hear from ~16 Hz to ~20,000 Hz. Dogs hear higher than us; bats "talk" at up to 212,000 Hz — a whole world of sound we never notice!

    High frequency = high pitchBirdsong ~4,000 Hz · a mosquito ~600 Hz · bats up to 212,000 Hz.
    Low frequency = low pitchThunder ~20–120 Hz · a big drum ~60 Hz · blue whales down to ~14 Hz.

    3Reading pitch from a wave picture

    You can read pitch straight from a wave picture: waves SQUEEZED tightly together = many vibrations per second = high frequency = HIGH pitch. Waves SPREAD far apart = few per second = low frequency = LOW pitch. Remember sound's two dials: the wave's HEIGHT → volume (unit 2.2); the wave's CLOSENESS → pitch (this unit). Independent dials — turning one leaves the other alone!

    4Pitch in the real world

    The general law: SMALL, SHORT, TIGHT things vibrate fast → high pitch; BIG, LONG, LOOSE things vibrate slowly → low pitch. Hence: a sparrow sings higher than a crow; a child's voice is higher than Dad's (shorter vocal cords); the piano's left keys (long strings) rumble lower than the right keys (short strings). Look at a sound source's size, and you can PREDICT its pitch before you hear it!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Wave X shows 3 ripples in a frame; wave Y shows 12 ripples in the same frame, at the same height. Compare the two sounds' pitch and volume.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Ripples in the same frame compare frequency.
    2. Height compares volume.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Y has 4× the frequency of X, so Y is much HIGHER in pitch; equal heights mean equal VOLUME. Pitch differs, loudness matches!
    Example 2

    The orchestra's note A is 440 Hz. What does that number actually say about the violin string playing it?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What does Hz count, and over what time?
    2. 440 of… what exactly?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the string swings back and forth exactly 440 times EVERY SECOND. Your ear receives 440 air-pushes per second, and your brain hears the note A. Frequency = vibrations per second.
    Example 3

    A dog whistle seems to make "no sound at all" — yet the dog comes running. Explain using frequency.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Human ears stop at ~20,000 Hz.
    2. Where does the dog whistle's frequency sit relative to that?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the whistle makes a real sound — but at a frequency ABOVE 20,000 Hz, over the human hearing ceiling. Dog ears reach ~45,000 Hz, so the dog hears it loud and clear. "Silent" only means silent to US!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Way 1: change the force — hit harder or softer

    Want a LOUDER sound? Feed the vibration more energy: hit harder, pluck harder, blow harder. Bigger force → bigger amplitude → louder sound. Want it QUIETER? Touch it softer — smaller vibration, gentler sound. This is how musicians control every note’s volume: same key, different force, different feeling!

    2Way 2: change the distance

    Cannot change the source? Change YOUR position! Nearer the source, the louder it is; farther away, the wave energy spreads thinner — the sound fades. That is why front-row concert seats feel so powerful, and stepping back from a speaker is an instant volume-down. Distance is the volume knob your feet control!

    3Way 3: block it or funnel it

    To QUIETEN sound: soft, spongy materials absorb its energy — blankets, curtains and foam muffle it. Studios line their walls with insulation; earmuffs wrap padding around your ears. To make sound LOUDER one way: a megaphone gathers waves that would spread everywhere into a single beam — no extra energy, just AIMED energy, like squeezing a hose into a jet.

    Soft and spongy = absorbs soundBlankets, carpets, curtains, foam — noise sinks in and vanishes.
    Hard and flat = bounces soundTiles, glass, bare walls — that is why bathrooms echo!

    4Sound engineering all around us

    Humans engineer volume every day: the volume knob tells the speaker cone to vibrate bigger or smaller; cinemas line walls with absorbing panels so movie sound stays crisp; motorways get noise walls to protect neighbourhoods; parents close the door while you sleep. Every trick uses one of the three ways: change the force, change the distance, or block/funnel the wave’s path.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna wants her xylophone note twice as loud WITHOUT changing the note. What should she do, and what happens to the vibration?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The note (pitch) is set by the bar — keep the same bar.
    2. Volume is set by amplitude — how do you enlarge it?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: strike the same bar HARDER. More force gives the bar a bigger amplitude → louder sound; the bar’s vibration speed is unchanged, so the note stays the same.
    Example 2

    The school band practises in a tiled room and the echo is awful. The teacher brings in thick curtains and some carpets. Why does this work?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What do hard tiles do to sound waves?
    2. What do soft, spongy curtains and carpets do to them?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: hard tiles BOUNCE sound waves back and forth, creating echo. Soft curtains and carpets ABSORB the sound energy — waves sink into the spongy fibres instead of rebounding. Less reflection, less echo, clearer music.
    Example 3

    The coach shouts through a megaphone and the whole field hears — but the megaphone has no battery or electricity. How does it "amplify"?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Without the megaphone, which directions does the voice spread in?
    2. What does the cone do to those directions?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: normally the voice spreads in ALL directions — most energy flies off uselessly. The cone FUNNELS all the waves into one forward beam: same energy, but concentrated one way, so it sounds much louder there. Aimed, not added!

    Practice

    Theory

    1A string's three pitch dials

    A string's pitch has THREE dials: (1) Length — a SHORT string vibrates fast → HIGH note; pressing a fret shortens the string and raises the note. (2) Tension — a tight string vibrates fast → high; a loose one → low; that is exactly how you tune. (3) Thickness — a thin string is light and quick → high; a thick, heavy one → low.

    2Wind instruments: the air column

    Flutes, recorders and trumpets have no strings — what vibrates is the air column inside the tube! The law matches strings exactly: a SHORT air column vibrates fast → HIGH note; a LONG column → LOW note. Covering more recorder holes = lengthening the column = deeper notes. Pouring water into a bottle = shrinking the air space = the glug rising higher. A whole orchestra in a water bottle!

    Short tube / column → high noteThe tiny piccolo trills above the whole orchestra.
    Long tube / column → low noteThe tuba coils metres of tube for its thunder-deep notes.

    3The golden rule: small-short-tight-thin = high

    Roll it all into one golden rule: SMALL, SHORT, TIGHT, THIN things vibrate FAST → HIGH pitch. BIG, LONG, LOOSE, THICK things vibrate SLOWLY → LOW pitch. Check it everywhere: the small violin sings high, the giant double bass hums low; the xylophone's short bar goes "ting", the long bar goes "tong"; a glass with little water differs from a full one. One rule — the whole world of instruments!

    4Your voice: the built-in instrument

    You carry an instrument everywhere: your voice box! Singing a HIGH note, tiny muscles pull your vocal cords TIGHTER (so they vibrate faster — the string law again). LOW notes = cords relax looser. Dad's voice is deeper because adult vocal cords are longer and thicker than a child's. Try it now: sing "do-re-mi" upward and feel your throat adjust!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna plucks an open guitar string, then presses her finger on the 5th fret and plucks again. Is the second note higher or lower? Why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Does pressing the fret make the VIBRATING part of the string longer or shorter?
    2. Does a shorter string vibrate faster or slower?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: higher. Her finger divides the string so only the part from fret to bridge vibrates — a SHORTER length vibrates FASTER → higher frequency → higher note.
    Example 2

    Nyna lines up 4 identical bottles: A full of water, B two-thirds, C one-third, D empty. She BLOWS across each top. Which bottle sounds HIGHEST? (Careful — blowing differs from tapping!)

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. When BLOWING, the vibrating thing is the AIR column above the water.
    2. Which bottle has the SHORTEST air column?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: bottle A (fullest). Water fills most of the space, so its air column is SHORTEST → fastest vibration → highest note. Empty D has the longest column → lowest. (TAPPING reverses the order — then the glass + water vibrates instead!)
    Example 3

    Nyna's guitar is flat — its A string sounds slightly LOWER than the standard 440 Hz. Which way must she turn the tuning peg, and what happens inside the string?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The note is too low — it must vibrate FASTER.
    2. Which string dial speeds vibration: length, tension, or thickness?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: turn the peg to TIGHTEN the string. Extra tension makes it vibrate faster — the frequency climbs up to 440 Hz. (The peg cannot change the string's length or thickness!)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Everything is made of particles

    ​Matter is everything that takes up space and has mass — tables, water, and the air you are breathing. The big secret: it is all built from particles — bricks so tiny that one water drop holds billions of billions. We cannot see single particles, so scientists use a model — a simple picture drawing particles as little balls — to explain how matter behaves.

    2Three states, three particle dances

    ​Solid: particles pack in neat rows, holding hands tightly, only VIBRATING in place → keeps its shape. Liquid: particles still touch but SLIDE past each other → flows, takes the container's shape. Gas: particles let go completely and FLY freely with big empty gaps → spreads to fill any space. Same particles — different dance!

    3Gas: the spreading champion

    Gas particles fly straight, crash and rebound in every direction — hundreds of metres per second! That is why a gas: (1) spreads through its whole container — perfume from one corner soon owns the room; (2) has no shape of its own; (3) can be compressed — the big gaps between particles let you squeeze them closer, like pumping a bike tyre. Solids and liquids barely compress — their particles already touch!

    Gas: fills everything + squeezableThe big gaps between particles explain both properties.
    Solid/liquid: already "full"Particles touch — squeeze all you like, they hardly shrink.

    4Air is real — even though invisible

    You cannot see air, but the particle model proves it is real matter: wave your hand — you FEEL billions of gas particles hitting your face; squeeze a sealed plastic bottle — the air inside PUSHES BACK; weigh a pumped-up ball — it is HEAVIER than a flat one. Gas takes space, has mass, and pushes — all the official ID of true matter!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna pours 200 ml of water from a round cup into a square box. The water's shape changes, but its volume is still 200 ml. Use the particle model to explain both facts.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What can liquid particles do that solid particles cannot?
    2. Do the particles move farther apart when changing cups?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: liquid particles SLIDE past one another, so the water flows into the new box shape — hence the shape changes. But the particles still touch closely, neither spreading out nor squeezing — so the total volume stays exactly 200 ml.
    Example 2

    Mum bakes a cake in the kitchen. Minutes later, Nyna smells it up in her bedroom. Tell the smell's journey using the particle model.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The smell is made of what, escaping the cake?
    2. How do gas particles travel through air?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the hot cake releases scent particles as a gas. They fly freely, colliding with air particles and rebounding in all directions — gradually spreading through the door, up the stairs, to Nyna's nose. Gases spread to fill every space!
    Example 3

    Nyna blocks her bike pump's nozzle and pushes the handle. It goes halfway down, then pushes back. She tries the pump full of water — the handle barely moves at all. Explain!

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What sits between gas particles? Between water particles?
    2. Which state can be compressed?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: air is a GAS — big gaps between particles let the pump squeeze them closer (compression), until they crowd tight and push back. Water is a LIQUID — its particles already touch, leaving no gaps to squeeze — so it hardly compresses at all.

    Practice

    Theory

    1One substance, three faces

    Water is the superstar of states: the very same H₂O particles can be solid ice, liquid water, or gaseous steam. What decides which face appears? Temperature! Heat is energy that makes particles jiggle and race faster: cold → slow particles holding hands → solid; warm → sliding particles → liquid; hot → particles breaking free and flying → gas.

    2Two golden numbers: 0°C and 100°C

    Measured with a thermometer on the Celsius scale, water has two magic marks: melting point = 0°C — below it water freezes; above it ice melts. Boiling point = 100°C — here water boils furiously into steam. These numbers are so reliable that the Celsius scale itself was BUILT on them!

    3Strange truth: the boiling point can shift

    100°C is only true at SEA LEVEL. Up a high mountain, the thinner air presses down less on the water → particles escape more easily → water boils at a LOWER temperature (on Fansipan ~89°C, on Everest ~70°C!). So mountain water "boils" without being fully hot — eggs take far longer to cook. The 0°C melting point, though, stays nearly the same everywhere.

    At sea level: boils at 100°CThick air presses hard — particles need full heat to escape.
    High mountains: boils below 100°CThin air — water boils "early", cooking runs slow.

    4Water's superpower: floating ice

    Most matter shrinks when it freezes — but water does the OPPOSITE: freezing locks its particles into a lattice full of empty spaces, making ice EXPAND and become ~9% lighter than liquid water. Result: ice FLOATS! It sounds small, but it saves the planet: floating lake ice acts like a blanket, keeping the water below unfrozen — fish and pond life survive the winter.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    The outdoor thermometer reads −5°C. Nyna leaves a cup of water on the balcony overnight. What state is it in by morning? Why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Compare −5°C with the melting/freezing point of 0°C.
    2. Below 0°C, what do water particles do?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the water has frozen solid. −5°C is below 0°C — under the freezing point, water particles slow down and lock into a solid lattice. (And since ice expands, the glass might even crack!)
    Example 2

    A pot of water boils hard at 100°C. Mum turns the flame to MAXIMUM. Does the water go above 100°C? Where does the extra heat go?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. At the boiling point, what job does extra heat do for the particles?
    2. Does the water boil harder, or hotter?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: no — liquid water stops at 100°C. All the extra heat goes into ripping particles free as steam: the water boils more violently and evaporates faster, but gets no hotter. (That is why max flame just wastes gas when boiling noodles!)
    Example 3

    Nyna's uncle, camping on Fansipan (3,147 m), complains: "The water is boiling but my noodles stay undercooked!" Explain it to him.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Is the air thick or thin at altitude?
    2. Does the boiling point rise or fall? How hot is "boiling" water up there?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: on Fansipan the thin air presses less, so water boils at only ~89°C. It IS boiling — but cooler than the 100°C of the lowlands, so noodles cook slowly. Fix: boil longer (or use a pressure cooker to push the boiling point back up!).

    Practice

    Theory

    1Evaporation: the quiet escape

    Water does NOT need to boil to become gas! Evaporation happens quietly at any temperature: at the liquid's surface, the fastest particles break free from their friends and fly up as invisible water vapour. That is why puddles dry by themselves and laundry drips dry. Want FASTER evaporation? Add sunshine (faster particles), add wind (carries vapour away), spread a bigger surface.

    Evaporation speeds up with:More heat · more wind · more surface — perfect laundry weather!
    Evaporation ≠ boilingBoiling: the whole liquid bubbles at 100°C. Evaporation: surface only, at any temperature.

    2Condensation: the return journey

    ​Condensation is the reverse trip: water vapour MEETS COLD, its particles slow down, huddle together, and return to liquid. Evidence is everywhere: the "sweat" on an iced-tea glass (air vapour touching the cold glass), the fogged bathroom mirror after a hot shower, the dew on morning grass after a cool night. One-sentence rule: vapour + cold surface = water drops.

    3The water cycle: Earth's forever machine

    Join the two processes and add gravity — you get the water cycle: (1) the Sun EVAPORATES sea and lake water into the sky; (2) up high it meets cold and CONDENSES into billions of tiny droplets — that IS a cloud; (3) droplets grow until too heavy, then fall: precipitation — rain, snow, hail; (4) water runs back to rivers and seas… and the loop restarts. Running nonstop for 4 billion years!

    4What a cloud is (and is not)

    A cloud is NOT water vapour — vapour is invisible! A cloud is billions of tiny LIQUID droplets (or ice crystals) that have already condensed, so small and light they float in the air. Vapour only becomes visible once it condenses into droplets: the plume over hot phở, your winter breath, and the clouds in the sky — all tiny liquid drops, not gas. True gas can never be seen!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Mum hangs two identical towels: one folded in four in still shade, one spread wide in sunny wind. Which dries first? Give ALL THREE reasons.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What are the three evaporation boosters?
    2. How many does the spread-out towel enjoy?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the spread-out sunny one — it enjoys all three boosters: (1) HEAT from sun speeds the particles, (2) WIND sweeps the vapour away continuously, (3) a wide SURFACE lets more particles escape at once. The folded shady towel misses all three — it may still be damp by evening!
    Example 2

    Nyna takes a soda can from the fridge. Minutes later the can is dripping wet. Her brother says it is leaking. Clear the can's name!

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Is the can colder or warmer than the air?
    2. What invisible thing is already in the air around it?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: no leak! Air always carries invisible water vapour. Touching the COLD can, vapour particles slow down and condense into droplets — the water comes from the AIR, not from inside. (Proof: the soda level inside has not dropped.)
    Example 3

    A water drop in Hạ Long Bay wants to "travel" and become rain on Fansipan's peak. Tell its journey through all 4 stations of the water cycle.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Station 1: how does it leave the sea surface?
    2. Station 2: what happens up high? Station 3: how does it fall? Station 4: where next?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) Sun warms the bay — the drop EVAPORATES into invisible vapour and rises; (2) winds carry it high and west, where cold makes it CONDENSE into a cloud; (3) the cloud droplet grows heavy and FALLS as mountain rain; (4) streams and rivers RUN the water back to the sea — ready for the next tour!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Where does the sugar "disappear" to?

    Stir sugar into water — it vanishes?! Not at all. It dissolves: water particles pull the sugar particles apart and surround each one, spreading them evenly through the glass. The sugar is still there — taste it! The result is a solution: a transparent, perfectly even mixture, equally sweet in every sip.

    2The vocabulary trio: solute, solvent, solution

    Three words, one formula: the solute — the thing that GETS dissolved (sugar, salt). The solvent — the liquid that DOES the dissolving (usually water — the "universal solvent"). Solute + solvent = solution. Example: salt water = salt (solute) + water (solvent). Fizzy drinks even dissolve a GAS — CO₂ — into water!

    Solute + solvent → solutionSugar + tea → sweet tea. Salt + water → salt water.
    Dissolving ≠ melting!Melting needs HEAT (ice → water). Dissolving needs a SOLVENT (sugar "vanishing" into water).

    3Soluble and insoluble

    Not everything agrees to dissolve! Soluble: sugar, salt — they form transparent solutions. Insoluble: sand, flour, chalk — stir all day and you only get a cloudy mixture or a sunken layer. To separate a mixture: a filter traps the insoluble bits. But filtering CANNOT catch dissolved substances — salt slips straight through filter paper! To get salt back? Let the water evaporate away.

    4Speeding up dissolving

    Three tricks to make a solute "vanish" faster — you use them daily without noticing: (1) STIR — brings fresh water to meet the solute nonstop; (2) HOT WATER — faster water particles collide harder and pull the solute apart quicker (that is why sugar dissolves faster in hot tea than iced tea!); (3) CRUSH IT SMALL — grains dissolve faster than cubes because the total contact surface is far bigger. All three tricks increase the "meetings" between water and solute particles.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna makes lemonade: she stirs sugar into lime juice and water. Identify the solute, the solvent, and the solution in her drink.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What GETS dissolved?
    2. Which liquid DOES the dissolving?
    3. What is the finished product called?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: sugar is the SOLUTE (the thing dissolved); the water + lime juice is the SOLVENT (the liquid doing the dissolving); the finished sweet lemonade is the SOLUTION.
    Example 2

    Nyna stirs a spoon of salt AND a spoon of sand into one glass of water. How can she get EACH one back separately? (Hint: it takes 2 different steps!)

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Sand never dissolved — which tool catches it?
    2. The salt is dissolved and slips through filters — how do you send the water away and keep the salt?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: step 1 — FILTER: the insoluble sand is trapped on the filter paper while the clear salt water runs through. Step 2 — EVAPORATE: leave the salt water in the sun (or warm it); the water evaporates away, leaving salt crystals behind. Vietnamese salt farmers do exactly this in their salt fields!
    Example 3

    Dissolving race: a sugar cube in still iced water versus grain sugar in stirred hot tea. Which wins? Name ALL the winner's advantages.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Recall the three dissolving boosters.
    2. How many does the hot tea side have?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the stirred hot tea with grain sugar wins by a mile, holding all THREE boosters: (1) HOT water — faster, harder-hitting particles; (2) STIRRING — fresh water keeps arriving; (3) SMALL grains — many times the cube's contact surface. The cube in still iced water could take an hour!

    Practice

    Theory

    1The nine-metre tube inside you

    ​Digestion happens in one continuous ~9-metre tube running through your body — from mouth to the end of the large intestine. Each section is an organ with its own job, linked like stations on a railway line: Mouth → Oesophagus → Stomach → Small intestine → Large intestine. A meal takes 1–3 DAYS to ride the whole line!

    2Stations 1–2: mouth and oesophagus

    At the mouth, a trio works: teeth cut and grind — sharp front teeth slice, flat molars mill; the tongue tastes, mixes and pushes; saliva wets the food and STARTS digesting starch (chew bread long enough and it turns sweet!). Swallowed, the food ball enters the oesophagus — a muscular tube that SQUEEZES food down in waves, so strongly you could swallow upside-down!

    3Station 3: the stomach — the churning machine

    The stomach is a stretchy muscular bag — a tiny washing machine: it kneads, squeezes and churns food with juices containing strong acid (strong enough to dissolve an iron nail — yet a special mucus lining protects the stomach itself!). After a few hours, the meal becomes a soupy liquid, ready for the most important station of all.

    4Stations 4–5: small and large intestine

    The small intestine — "small" because it is NARROW, not short: it coils ~6 metres! Here the food's treasure — nutrients — passes through the intestine wall into the BLOOD to feed the whole body. The large intestine is wider but shorter (~1.5 m): it reclaims WATER from what is left and packs up the waste. Named for WIDTH, not length — don't let the names fool you!

    Small intestine = narrow but LONG (6 m)The nutrient-absorbing station — the system's superstar.
    Large intestine = wide but SHORT (1.5 m)The water-reclaiming and waste-packing station.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Tell the journey of a bite of rice from entering the mouth until its nutrients reach the blood — naming the first 4 stations in the right order.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which station chews and wets?
    2. Which tube squeezes down? Which bag churns?
    3. In which long tube do nutrients enter the blood?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) MOUTH — teeth grind, saliva softens and starts digesting; (2) OESOPHAGUS — squeezes the food ball down; (3) STOMACH — churns it with acid into "soup"; (4) SMALL INTESTINE — nutrients pass through its wall into the blood.
    Example 2

    Riddle: the SMALL intestine is 6 metres long; the LARGE intestine only 1.5 metres. Why does the much longer one get called "small"?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Are the names based on LENGTH or WIDTH?
    2. Compare the two tubes' diameters.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the names refer to WIDTH (diameter)! The small intestine is narrow (~2.5 cm) but coils very long; the large intestine is wide (~7 cm) but short. "Small/large" describes the tube's width, not its length.
    Example 3

    Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve an iron nail. So why doesn't the stomach digest ITSELF?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What coats the stomach's walls?
    2. How often is that coating renewed?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the stomach wall coats itself with a thick MUCUS layer — an acid-proof raincoat — and constantly renews it. Thanks to that self-refreshing shield, the "acid washing machine" digests only the meal — never itself.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The big mission: meal into fuel

    Why digest at all? Because a bite of rice or fish is far TOO BIG for a cell to use! The system's mission: break down food into tiny nutrients, load them into the blood for delivery to every cell — where they become fuel for running and thinking, and BUILDING MATERIAL for growing. The unusable part leaves as waste.

    2Two kinds of breakdown: mechanical and chemical

    The system attacks food on two fronts: MECHANICAL — teeth grind and the stomach churns: physically smashing pieces smaller, like crushing a brick. CHEMICAL — acid dissolves food and kills germs; enzymes work like chemical scissors, snipping food molecules small enough to slip into the blood. The fronts cooperate: mechanical crushing first makes the chemical scissors work many times faster!

    Mechanical: teeth + churningPHYSICALLY smashing pieces — widening the surface for chemistry.
    Chemical: acid + enzymesSnipping MOLECULES tiny enough to enter the blood.

    3Peristalsis: the muscle conveyor belt

    Food does not flow by itself — it is PUSHED. Peristalsis is waves of muscle contraction running along the tube: muscles BEHIND the food ball squeeze, muscles AHEAD relax — the ball gets "squeezed forward", exactly like pushing toothpaste from the bottom of the tube. Thanks to peristalsis you can swallow lying down, and astronauts can eat in space. The conveyor runs all 9 metres, day and night!

    4Delivery and cleanup

    At the small intestine, tiny nutrients pass through the wall into the blood — the delivery river carrying them to EVERY cell: muscles get fuel for running, the brain for thinking, bones get material for growing longer. Meanwhile mucus quietly protects the pipeline all along the route. What cannot be digested (like fibre) continues to the large intestine, becomes waste, and leaves the body. Nothing wasted, nothing jammed — a perfect factory!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Sort these into MECHANICAL or CHEMICAL breakdown: (a) teeth grinding an apple, (b) enzymes snipping starch into sugar, (c) the stomach churning, (d) acid dissolving meat.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Mechanical = physical force smashing.
    2. Chemical = special juices snipping molecules.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: MECHANICAL — (a) grinding teeth and (c) the churning stomach (physical force). CHEMICAL — (b) snipping enzymes and (d) dissolving acid (chemical reactions). Both fronts cooperate in every meal!
    Example 2

    Nyna lies flat on the sofa drinking milk — and it still reaches her stomach although she is horizontal. Which mechanism does this, and how does it work?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Gravity barely helps when horizontal.
    2. Remember the toothpaste-tube trick.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: peristalsis. The oesophagus muscles squeeze BEHIND the milk and relax AHEAD of it, pushing it along wave by wave like squeezing a toothpaste tube — no gravity required at all.
    Example 3

    Before an afternoon swim meet, the coach tells Nyna to eat a good lunch 2–3 hours beforehand. Using digestion's function, explain the advice.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. How long does food need to become nutrients in the blood?
    2. What must the swimming muscles receive by race time?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: digestion takes time! After 2–3 hours, lunch has been broken down and its nutrients are riding the blood — ready to fuel her muscles at race time. Eating too close to the race means a still-full stomach (heavy, crampy) with the fuel not yet delivered to the muscles.

    Practice

    Theory

    1What does "balanced" mean?

    Your body is a construction site working 24/7 — and each food delivers a different "material". A balanced diet means: ENOUGH kinds (variety), the RIGHT amounts (sensible portions), at REGULAR times (steady meals). No single food is a "superfood" that does everything — and no food needs banning outright. The secret is in the proportions!

    2Why VARIETY matters

    Every food carries its own "gift box": fish brings protein; rice brings energy; greens bring fibre and vitamins; milk brings calcium — a bone-building mineral. NO single food contains everything! Eating one food forever — even a "good" one — still leaves gaps. The easy colour rule: the more NATURAL COLOURS on the plate (green, red, orange, yellow, purple), the more complete your vitamin collection.

    3Portions and "treat foods"

    Balance is also about AMOUNTS. The famous target: 5 portions of fruit and veg a day (one portion ≈ your own fist). Junk food — sweets, chips, fizzy drinks — needs no total ban, but it is an OCCASIONAL TREAT, not daily fuel: rich in sugar and fat, poor in vitamins and fibre. And never forget the most important drink: WATER, which makes up more than half your body!

    Daily: grains, veg, protein, fruit, waterFuel and building material for a growing body.
    Occasionally: sweets, chips, fizzy drinksTasty but nutrient-poor — keep them in the "treat" role.

    4Balance changes with the person

    "Balanced" is not one rigid recipe for everyone! A swimmer in heavy training needs more energy foods (rice, noodles) than an office worker. A growing child like you needs extra calcium and protein for building bones and muscles. Someone ill needs extra water and vitamins. The principle is shared — all the groups, sensible amounts — but each person's "dose" differs with age, activity and health.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Score this dinner tray for balance: white rice, braised fish, rau ngót soup, watermelon for dessert. Which groups are present? Anything missing?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Check the five groups: grains, protein, vegetables, fruit, dairy.
    2. Which dish covers which group?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: a very high score! Rice = grains; fish = protein; soup greens = vegetables; watermelon = fruit. Four groups present — only DAIRY is missing (add a glass of milk or a yogurt). The traditional Vietnamese tray is naturally balanced!
    Example 2

    Nyna's friend declares: "Apples are the healthiest food, so I will eat ONLY apples every day to be healthy." Use the idea of variety to find the flaw.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which gift box do apples carry? Which are missing?
    2. Where would protein and calcium come from on apples alone?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: apples are good but carry only ONE gift box (vitamins, fibre, some sugar). Apples alone means no protein for muscles, no calcium for bones, no fats for the brain… No food can carry everything — health comes from a COLLECTION of foods, not one superstar.
    Example 3

    Nyna picks a pre-swim snack: (a) a bag of gummy sweets, or (b) a banana and a yogurt. Analyse both options nutritionally.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What do gummies carry besides sugar?
    2. Which nutrient groups do banana + yogurt bring?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) gummies = fast sugar, no vitamins, no protein — an energy spike then a slump. (b) the banana gives steady energy + potassium (a muscle-helping mineral); yogurt adds protein and calcium. Option (b) fuels the swim smoothly and long — save the sweets as an occasional AFTER-practice treat!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Carbohydrates: the energy team

    ​Carbohydrates are the body's main fuel, arriving in two styles: starch — in rice, potatoes and bread — burns SLOWLY and steadily like a big log, powering you for hours; sugar — in sweets and soda — burns FAST like straw: a quick blaze, then gone. The body breaks every carbohydrate into simple sugars to "burn" — but the burn speed decides how full and focused you feel!

    2Proteins and fats: builders and reserves

    ​Protein — in fish, meat, eggs, tofu and beans — is the BUILDING CREW: it builds muscle, repairs wounds, makes hair and nails. Growing children need protein daily! Fat — in oils, butter, oily fish and nuts — is dense energy storage and BRAIN-building material; truly necessary, but only in small amounts. Protein builds, fat stores and protects — the quiet teams behind every centimetre you grow.

    3Dairy, vitamins and minerals

    ​Dairy — milk, yogurt, cheese — is famous for calcium: the "cement" mineral for bones and teeth. Other micronutrients hold specialist jobs too: iron in meat and dark greens helps blood carry oxygen; vitamin A serves the eyes; vitamin C boosts defences (remember the sailors!); vitamin D helps absorb calcium itself. The amounts needed are tiny — but missing one makes the body misfire fast.

    Quick duty rosterCarbs → energy · Protein → building · Fat → brain + reserves · Calcium → bones · Iron → blood.
    No group substitutes for anotherExtra rice cannot cover a protein gap — each team has its own trade!

    4Reading a meal with food-group eyes

    Now you own "analysis glasses" — try reading a bowl of phở bò: the rice noodles = carbohydrate (energy); the beef = protein (builders) + iron (blood); the bone broth = a little fat + minerals; the herbs and bean sprouts = vitamins + fibre. One bowl covers nearly every group! This skill works at every meal: name each dish's group, and you will instantly see what the meal lacks or overloads.

    Answer: rice = carbohydrate (starch); braised fish = protein; cooking oil = fat; yogurt = dairy (calcium); rau muống = vegetables (vitamins, iron, fibre). This tray covers all five groups!

    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: rice is STARCH — long chains that must be snipped gradually, releasing sugar steadily for hours (the big log). Candy is simple SUGAR — absorbed instantly, a quick blaze then a crash (burning straw). Same carbohydrate family, opposite burn speeds!
