    Nyna is 10 and growing fast. Which TWO "building materials" should she focus on most — and in which foods will she find them?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Growing fast = lengthening bones + growing muscles.
    2. Which team builds muscle? Which mineral cements bone?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) PROTEIN for muscles and every growing tissue — from fish, eggs, meat, tofu and milk; (2) CALCIUM for the lengthening skeleton — from milk, yogurt, cheese and small shrimp. (Plus vitamin D — morning sunshine! — so the calcium gets absorbed well.)

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a force? Pushes and pulls!

    A force is simply a push or a pull. Forces can make objects: START moving (kick a ball), STOP (catch it), CHANGE DIRECTION (head it), speed UP or slow DOWN, and even CHANGE SHAPE (squash a can). Force is measured in newtons (N) — named after the famous scientist Isaac Newton. Holding an average apple? You are supporting about 1 N of weight!

    2Gravity: the pull that never rests

    ​Gravity is Earth's PULL on everything, towards its centre — no touching needed, never switched off. It keeps your feet on the ground, pulls the rain down, and even holds the Moon in orbit! Your weight is exactly gravity's pull on your body, measured in newtons. Drop anything — gravity wins, every time.

    3The resisting trio: friction, air and water resistance

    A whole family of forces WORKS AGAINST motion: friction — born when two surfaces rub; both a friend (shoes grip, brakes work) and a nuisance (machines heat up and wear out). Air resistance — friction with air: the parachutist's saviour, the racing cyclist's enemy. Water resistance — far stronger than air's; that is why boats and fish are streamlined. All three grow stronger the faster you move!

    Friction is a FRIEND when:Walking without slipping · brakes gripping · holding things firmly.
    Friction is a NUISANCE when:Machines overheat and wear · athletes need maximum speed.

    4Upthrust — and how to name any force

    ​Upthrust is water's UPWARD PUSH on objects — it fights gravity and keeps boats, floats, and you yourself on top of the pool. To identify any force, ask three detective questions: (1) Push or pull? (2) Which direction? (3) Who causes it — the Earth (gravity), rubbing surfaces (friction), air, water, or a hand? Answer those and every force reveals its name!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Name the main force in each scene: (a) a mango dropping from its branch; (b) a bike skidding to a stop; (c) a leaf drifting down slowly; (d) a float bobbing on the pool.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Who pulls the mango down? Who eats the wheel's speed?
    2. Why does a leaf fall slower than a stone? Who lifts the float?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) gravity pulls the mango down; (b) friction between tyre and road stops the bike; (c) air resistance slows the drifting leaf; (d) upthrust from the water lifts the float.
    Example 2

    Nyna notices two odd things: a freshly mopped floor is dangerously slippery, yet a rubber door handle is easy to grip and turn. ONE force explains both — which, and why the opposite effects?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What does the water layer do between floor and shoe?
    2. Does grippy rubber make much or little friction?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: friction! Mop water forms a slippery layer that REDUCES friction — shoes lose grip, falls happen. Textured rubber INCREASES friction — hands grip the handle firmly. Low friction = slide; high friction = grip. One force, two faces!
    Example 3

    Drop two identical paper sheets together: one flat, one crumpled into a ball. The ball lands first. Gravity pulls both equally — so what makes the difference?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. How much air does the flat sheet catch compared with the ball?
    2. Which force grows with the wind-catching area?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: air resistance. The flat sheet's large area catches lots of air — big resistance fighting gravity, so it falls slowly and flutters. The compact ball meets little resistance — it drops fast and straight. That is precisely the parachute's secret: INCREASE the area to increase the resistance!

    Practice

    Theory

    1The language of arrows

    Forces are invisible — so scientists DRAW them! In a force diagram, the object becomes a simple box, and every force acting on it becomes an arrow carrying three facts: (1) direction — the arrow points the way the force acts; (2) size — the LONGER the arrow, the stronger the force; (3) a label — the force's name and its newtons. One drawing says a thousand words!

    2Balanced: when arrows cancel

    When two forces are EQUAL in size and OPPOSITE in direction — like 500 N of weight pulling a boat down and 500 N of upthrust lifting it — they are balanced: they cancel completely. The result? Motion does NOT change: a still object stays still (the boat floats in place), a steadily moving object keeps cruising. The diagram tells you at a glance: two opposing arrows of equal length = balance.

    3Unbalanced: someone wins

    When the arrows are NOT equal — 70 N pushing one way, 30 N resisting — the forces are unbalanced. The difference is the resultant: 70 − 30 = 40 N toward the stronger side. A resultant CHANGES motion: speeding up, slowing down, or turning. Tug-of-war is a living force diagram: the stronger team creates a resultant toward themselves — and the rope slides their way!

    Balanced → motion unchangedStill stays still · steady stays steady.
    Unbalanced → motion changesResultant = the difference, pointing toward the stronger side.

    4Drawing a proper force diagram

    The scientist's four steps: (1) Draw the object as a plain box (skip the details!); (2) List every force acting — ask: gravity? friction? who pushes/pulls? water/air?; (3) Draw one arrow per force FROM the object, in the right direction, length matching size; (4) Label with name + newtons. Final check: do the arrows agree with the real motion? A still object needs arrows that balance!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A book rests STILL on a table. Draw its force diagram: which forces act, and how must the arrows look?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Gravity pulls the book down — yet it does not fall through the table. Who holds it up?
    2. The book is still → how must the two arrows compare?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: two arrows — the weight (gravity) pointing DOWN, and the table's support force pushing UP. Since the book stays still, the arrows must be EQUAL in length and opposite: balanced forces, unchanged motion.
    Example 2

    Tug-of-war: team Red pulls left with 260 N, team Blue pulls right with 300 N. Find the resultant and predict what happens.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Opposite directions → take the difference.
    2. Toward which team does the resultant point?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: resultant = 300 − 260 = 40 N to the right (Blue's side). Unbalanced forces → motion changes: the rope (and poor team Red) slides steadily toward team Blue!
    Example 3

    A rocket weighing 5,000 N fires engines producing 7,000 N of upward thrust. Draw the two arrows, find the resultant, and say whether it lifts off.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Up arrow: 7,000 N. Down arrow: 5,000 N. Which is longer?
    2. What is the difference, and which way?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the thrust arrow (7,000 N up) is longer than the weight arrow (5,000 N down). Resultant = 2,000 N UPWARD — an unbalanced force changes motion: the rocket accelerates off the pad! (With only 5,000 N of thrust — balanced — it would roar but sit still.)

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a satellite? What is an orbit?

    A satellite is ANY object that travels around a planet. Its repeating path is called an orbit. Who keeps a satellite on its orbit? An old friend from lesson 5.1: gravity! Earth constantly pulls the Moon towards itself; but because the Moon is racing sideways so fast, that pull only bends its path into a giant circle — it never crashes down, and never flies away. It is like swinging a ball on a string around your head: the string of gravity keeps the Moon-ball circling forever.

    2Natural satellites: our Moon

    A natural satellite is made by nature. The Moon is Earth's ONLY natural satellite — a ball of rock that circles us about once a month (28 days). It makes no light of its own; moonlight is really reflected sunlight! Other planets have much bigger moon families: Mars has 2, and Jupiter has more than 90 moons! So the word satellite is not just for machines — the Moon is Earth's most senior satellite of all.

    3Artificial satellites: machines in the sky

    An artificial satellite is a machine BUILT by people and launched on a rocket. Since the very first, Sputnik 1 (1957 — only the size of a basketball!), THOUSANDS of satellites now circle Earth. Each has a job: weather satellites photograph storm clouds; communication satellites relay TV and phone signals (Vietnam has VINASAT-1 and VINASAT-2!); GPS satellites guide cars; space telescopes gaze at distant stars. And the biggest of all: the International Space Station (ISS) — an artificial satellite with people aboard, where astronauts live and work!

    NATURAL satellite:Made by nature · Earth has exactly 1: the Moon.
    ARTIFICIAL satellite:Built by people · thousands of them: weather, TV, GPS, the ISS…

    4Why don't satellites fall down?

    The best question of the lesson! Surprising truth: a satellite IS falling — but it is also moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. Imagine throwing a ball harder and harder: it lands further and further away. Throw it fast enough (about 28,000 km/h!) and Earth's curved surface drops away exactly as fast as the ball falls — so it falls AROUND the Earth forever. That is an orbit: a fall that never lands! Space has almost no air, so no air resistance slows the satellite down.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Sort these satellites into NATURAL or ARTIFICIAL: (a) the Moon; (b) Vietnam's VINASAT-1; (c) the International Space Station; (d) one of Jupiter's moons.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The only question to ask: did nature or people make it?
    2. A moon of ANOTHER planet is still a moon!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: NATURAL — (a) the Moon and (d) Jupiter's moon (made by nature). ARTIFICIAL — (b) VINASAT-1 and (c) the ISS (built and launched by people).
    Example 2

    Nyna's friend says: "There is no gravity in space — that is why satellites just float and never fall." Correct the science.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. If gravity truly switched off, would a satellite's path be straight or curved?
    2. Who bends the path into a circle?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Gravity IS still there — it is exactly what holds the satellite in orbit! Without gravity the satellite would fly off in a straight line into space. A satellite is really falling AROUND the Earth: gravity pulls it inward while its enormous sideways speed keeps it from ever hitting the ground.
    Example 3

    A storm is approaching the East Sea (biển Đông). Name TWO kinds of artificial satellite that help people in Vietnam in this situation, and say what each one does.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which kind of satellite can SEE the storm clouds from above?
    2. Which kind carries the warning broadcast to TVs and phones across the country?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) A WEATHER satellite photographs the storm from space, helping forecasters predict its path and strength. (2) A COMMUNICATION satellite (like VINASAT) carries the warning broadcast to TVs, radios and phones everywhere — even to fishing boats far out at sea.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Many forces act at the same time

    In real life, an object rarely feels just ONE force. A swimmer gets pushed UP by upthrust, pulled DOWN by gravity, pushed FORWARD by each kick, and pushed BACK by water resistance — four forces at once! The object does not feel each force separately; it only responds to the COMBINED effect of them all. So to predict what happens, we must combine the forces — just like adding and subtracting in maths!

    2Same direction: ADD. Opposite directions: SUBTRACT

    The force-combining rule has just two lines: forces in the SAME direction add — two friends each pushing a sofa with 100 N make one 200 N push. Forces in OPPOSITE directions subtract — a 200 N push forward against 50 N of friction leaves a 150 N resultant forward. This upgrades your force-diagram skill from lesson 5.2: now you can CALCULATE what the object will do!

    3Float or sink: weight versus upthrust

    Dropping an object into water starts a battle between two opposite forces: weight pulling down and upthrust pushing up. Upthrust wins or draws? The object floats. Weight wins? It sinks. Shape matters enormously: a crumpled foil ball sinks, yet the same foil spread into a boat floats — the wide hull pushes aside more water and earns more upthrust. And once an object MOVES through water, a third force joins in: water resistance pushing against the motion.

    FLOATS when:Upthrust ≥ weight — boats, floats, cooked bánh trôi.
    SINKS when:Weight > upthrust — coins, stones, anchors.

    4What can a resultant force do to motion?

    When forces are NOT balanced, the leftover resultant can do four things to motion: (1) speed it up — resultant along the motion, like pedalling hard; (2) slow it down — resultant against the motion, like squeezing the brakes; (3) change its direction — a sideways resultant, like kicking a rolling ball; (4) change the object's shape — like squashing a can. And when forces ARE balanced? Recall lesson 5.2: motion stays exactly as it was — still stays still, steady stays steady!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Two brothers push a crate forward together: one with 120 N, the other with 80 N. Friction with the floor resists with 150 N. Find the resultant force and say whether the crate moves.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The two pushes point the SAME way — which operation first?
    2. Then compare that total with the OPPOSITE friction force.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Add the same-direction pushes: 120 + 80 = 200 N forward. Subtract the opposing friction: 200 − 150 = 50 N forward. The 50 N resultant is not zero, so the crate MOVES — it speeds up forward.
    Example 2

    Nyna crumples a piece of foil into a ball — it sinks. She spreads an IDENTICAL piece into a little boat — it floats. Same material, same weight! Explain using the weight-versus-upthrust battle.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Is the weight of the two shapes any different?
    2. Which shape pushes aside more water when placed on the surface?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: The weight stays the same — but the UPTHRUST changes! The compact foil ball pushes aside very little water → weak upthrust → weight wins → it sinks. The wide boat displaces far more water → upthrust grows until it balances the weight → it floats. Shape decides the battle!
    Example 3

    A swimmer is gliding along the lane at a steady speed. Name the FOUR forces acting on her, give each force's direction, and explain why her speed is not changing.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which two forces act vertically? Which two act horizontally?
    2. What does a steady speed tell you about each pair?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) Weight pulls DOWN; (2) upthrust pushes UP; (3) her kick and arm stroke push FORWARD; (4) water resistance pushes BACKWARD. Her speed stays steady because each pair balances: upthrust = weight (she neither sinks nor pops up), stroke force = water resistance (she neither speeds up nor slows down). Four forces — resultant zero!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Magnets and their two poles

    A magnet is an object that makes a special pulling force — magnetism. It is the second force you have met that works AT A DISTANCE, no touching needed (what was the first? Gravity!). Every magnet, big or small, has exactly TWO poles: a north (N) pole — often painted red — and a south (S) pole. The magnetic force is strongest at the poles. Snap a magnet in half? You cannot separate the poles — each half grows both poles again, making two smaller magnets!

    2Attract and repel: the law of the poles

    Bring two magnets together and you feel the law of the poles: OPPOSITE poles (N meets S) attract — they leap together with a click! LIKE poles (N meets N, or S meets S) repel — you feel a springy invisible cushion between your hands. This repelling force is so special that maglev trains use it to FLOAT above the track, deleting wheel friction (remember lesson 5.1?) and flying along at over 600 km/h!

    OPPOSITES attract:N ↔ S leap together — click!
    LIKES repel:N ↔ N or S ↔ S — an invisible cushion pushes apart.

    3Which materials are magnetic? (The biggest trap!)

    Here is the lesson's biggest trap: NOT every metal is magnetic! Magnets strongly attract only iron, steel (because steel is made from iron), plus two rarer cousins, nickel and cobalt. But aluminium (drinks cans), copper (electric wires), gold and silver — all metals, yet a magnet IGNORES them completely! Wood, plastic, glass and paper are of course non-magnetic too. The only reliable test: BRING A MAGNET CLOSE and watch what happens.

    4The compass: Earth itself is a magnet!

    The grandest secret of magnetism: the Earth itself is a giant magnet, with magnetic poles near the North and South Poles. A compass needle is a tiny magnet balanced on a free-spinning pivot — the Earth-magnet pulls it around until it points north. For a thousand years compasses have guided explorers and fishermen — including Vietnamese fishing boats on the East Sea on starless nights. From fridge doors to compasses to maglev trains: this invisible push-and-pull force is at work all around you!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna tests a magnet on 6 objects: an iron nail, an aluminium can, a steel paper clip, a plastic spoon, a copper wire, and an eraser. Predict which ones the magnet attracts.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Golden rule: magnets attract only iron and steel (plus nickel and cobalt).
    2. Aluminium and copper are metals — but are they on the list?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: The magnet attracts only the IRON NAIL and the STEEL PAPER CLIP (steel contains iron). The aluminium can and copper wire are metals but NOT magnetic — the magnet ignores them. The plastic spoon and eraser, of course not. Metal ≠ magnetic!
    Example 2

    Two bar magnets lie on a table. Bringing the red end (N) of one magnet near one end of the other makes them spring APART. What is the OTHER end of the second magnet? Explain step by step.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Repelling means the two poles are ALIKE or opposite?
    2. Every magnet always has one N and one S.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Springing apart = REPEL = like poles. So the tested end of the second magnet is N (same as the red N end). Every magnet has exactly one N and one S, so its other end must be S. Detective reasoning: one repulsion reveals both ends!
    Example 3

    A paper clip falls into a glass of water. Dad challenges Nyna to get it out WITHOUT touching the water and without pouring it away. Nyna has a bar magnet. What should she do, and why does it work?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Does magnetic force pass through glass and water?
    2. What material is a paper clip made of?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Press the magnet against the OUTSIDE of the glass, level with the clip, then slide it slowly up to the rim — the steel clip follows along inside! It works because magnetic force acts AT A DISTANCE and passes through glass and water, and the clip is steel (contains iron), so it is attracted. Perfectly dry hands!

    Practice

    Theory

    1The Earth orbits the Sun

    Lesson 5.3 taught that the Moon is Earth's satellite. Now zoom out further: Earth itself is flying around something too — the Sun, our star! Its nearly circular path is Earth's orbit, and who holds it there? Gravity again — this time the Sun's colossal pull. Earth races along at about 107,000 km/h, yet we feel nothing, because everything around us — houses, air, oceans — glides along together perfectly smoothly.

    2Two movements: SPIN daily, ORBIT yearly

    Earth does TWO things at once — like a dancer spinning on the spot while also walking a circle around the stage. Job one: rotation — Earth spins around its axis, one turn every 24 hours = one day. Job two: revolution — Earth travels one full lap around the Sun in 365 days = one year. Never mix the words up: rotation is spinning ON THE SPOT, revolution is TRAVELLING AROUND something else!

    3365 days… and a quarter! Leap years

    The calendar's secret: one lap around the Sun really takes 365 days AND about a quarter (365.25 days). A calendar cannot print "a quarter day", so it SAVES UP: each year it keeps ¼ day back, and after 4 years it has collected ¼ × 4 = 1 whole day — which it gives to February as the 29th. That special 366-day year is a leap year. Without it the calendar would slowly drift — after a few centuries, New Year would land in… summer!

    ROTATION:Spin around the axis · 24 hours · makes DAY and NIGHT.
    REVOLUTION:Lap around the Sun · 365.25 days · makes the YEAR (and leap years).

    4The Sun — our very own star

    A star is a gigantic ball of glowing hot gas that makes its own light. The thousands of twinkling night stars are all faraway suns — ours is simply the one star CLOSE ENOUGH to warm your skin and light the day. For fun scale: more than a MILLION Earths could fit inside the Sun! It is the gravity of that giant — like an invisible string 150 million km long — that keeps Earth in its lane on the orbit, year after year, birthday after birthday.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Fill in "rotation" or "revolution": (a) the reason night follows day; (b) the reason birthdays come 365 days apart; (c) the movement that takes 24 hours; (d) the movement that takes 365 days.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Rotation = spinning on the spot around the axis; revolution = travelling around the Sun.
    2. Match each event to the fast movement (day) or the slow one (year).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) rotation — the side turning away from the Sun slips into night; (b) revolution — each birthday is one lap around the Sun; (c) rotation — 24 hours; (d) revolution — 365 days.
    Example 2

    An orbital year lasts 365.25 days, but a normal calendar prints only 365. Work out how many days the calendar "owes" after 4 years, and explain how the leap year pays the debt.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Each year the calendar is short by 365.25 − 365 = ? days.
    2. Multiply that shortfall by 4 years.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Each year the calendar falls 0.25 days behind. After 4 years: 0.25 × 4 = 1 whole day. The leap year pays it back by adding February 29th — that year has 366 days, and the calendar matches the orbit again!
    Example 3

    Nyna wonders: "If Earth is racing along at 107,000 km/h, why am I not blown away by wind or feeling dizzy?" Use the example of riding a smooth aeroplane (or train) to explain.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Inside a smooth plane, do you feel the 900 km/h? Why not?
    2. Does the air inside the plane travel with you or against you?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: In a smooth plane you pour water and walk about easily — because YOU, the SEAT and the AIR are all moving at the same speed; we only feel CHANGES of speed (take-off, bumps). Earth is the same: the ground, oceans, atmosphere and you all glide together perfectly smoothly at a nearly constant speed — so no wind blast, no dizziness. Steady motion that everything shares simply cannot be felt!

    Practice

    Theory

    1The Earth stands… tilted!

    Lesson 6.1 showed Earth spinning on its axis. The most important missing detail: that axis does NOT stand straight! Earth tilts at 23.5 degrees — like a spinning top leaning slightly to one side yet never falling. The magic part: throughout the whole lap around the Sun, the tilted axis keeps pointing THE SAME WAY in space. So sometimes the northern half leans TOWARDS the Sun, and half a year later it leans AWAY — and that slow nodding is exactly what creates the four seasons!

    2Why does leaning towards the Sun = summer?

    The hemisphere leaning TOWARDS the Sun receives two gifts at once. Gift one: sunlight strikes it more DIRECTLY — like a torch aimed straight at a wall making a small, brilliant circle; tilt the torch and the light spreads wide and weak. Gift two: LONGER days — the Sun rises earlier and sets later, giving extra hours of warming. Strong light + long days = rising temperature = summer. The other hemisphere, leaning away, gets slanted weak light and short days = winter.

    3Four seasons — and the great hemisphere swap

    Earth travels around the Sun while its tilted axis keeps its direction, so each hemisphere takes turns through four stages: spring — days lengthen, plants bud; summer — peak sunshine, the longest days; autumn — days shrink, leaves turn gold; winter — the shortest, coldest days. And here is the most delightful rule: the two hemispheres are ALWAYS in opposite seasons! When Hanoi welcomes summer, Australia shivers through winter; a white Christmas in Russia is blazing summer in the southern hemisphere.

    Leaning TOWARDS the Sun:Direct light + long days = SUMMER.
    Leaning AWAY from the Sun:Slanted weak light + short days = WINTER.

    4The equator — the land of "no winter"

    The equator — the imaginary belt around Earth's middle — barely feels the tilt: it receives fairly direct sunlight all year, so it stays warm with days and nights of roughly 12 hours each. Vietnam lies quite close to the equator, which is why the south (like Ho Chi Minh City) has just two seasons — rainy and dry — while the north, further from the equator, feels all four seasons distinctly. The further from the equator towards the poles, the more extreme the seasons get: at the poles there are summer "white nights" and winter days when the Sun never rises at all!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    In July, the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun. Give the season in: (a) Hanoi (northern hemisphere); (b) Sydney, Australia (southern hemisphere); (c) Singapore (right by the equator).

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Leaning towards the Sun = which season? And the other hemisphere?
    2. Does the equator really have four seasons at all?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) Hanoi — SUMMER (the northern hemisphere is leaning towards the Sun); (b) Sydney — WINTER (the southern hemisphere leans away — always the opposite season); (c) Singapore — warm as ever, because the equator barely feels the tilt.
    Example 2

    Use the torch experiment to explain: why is winter sunshine weaker than summer sunshine, when it comes from the very same Sun?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What does a straight-on torch beam look like? A tilted one?
    2. If the same light spreads over a bigger area, how much does each square metre get?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: In winter your hemisphere leans AWAY, so sunbeams arrive at a SLANT — like the tilted torch: the same light is spread across a much bigger area, so EACH square metre of ground receives only a small share. In summer the beams arrive nearly straight down — light concentrated onto a small area, each square metre getting far more heat. Same Sun, different angle!
    Example 3

    Nyna's friend says: "Summer is hot because the Earth travels CLOSER to the Sun." Use NASA's surprising fact (Earth is nearest the Sun in early January) to prove him wrong.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. In early January, which season is the northern hemisphere having?
    2. If distance were the cause, what season SHOULD January be in the north?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: If "closer = hotter" were true, early January — when Earth is NEAREST the Sun — should be peak summer everywhere. Yet January is the middle of WINTER in the northern hemisphere (and summer in the southern)! The distance change is far too small to cause seasons; the real culprit is the 23.5° TILT — which decides which hemisphere gets direct light and long days.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The Sun "rises" and "sets" — but who is really moving?

    Every morning the Sun appears at the eastern horizon — that is sunrise. Every evening it sinks in the west — sunset. But here is the sky's greatest trick: THE SUN IS NOT MOVING around us at all! It is the Earth's own spin (lesson 6.1) that turns you TOWARDS the Sun at dawn and AWAY from it at dusk. It is like riding a merry-go-round: the scenery seems to sweep past, but the one moving is you. Scientists call that looks-real-but-is-not path apparent motion.

    2Rises in the east, sets in the west — never once wrong

    Earth spins from west to east, so for anyone standing on the ground, the Sun always appears in the east and disappears in the west — every morning, every evening, everywhere on the planet. That is nature's free compass: fishermen, forest hikers and explorers all find their way by it. Sun on your right in the morning? Then you are heading south!

    3The shadow clock: long at dawn, short at noon

    As the Sun climbs the sky, every object's shadow changes with it — a natural clock! In the early morning the Sun sits low near the horizon: light arrives at a SLANT, shadows stretch LONG and point west. At noon / midday, the Sun stands HIGHEST: light falls nearly straight down and shadows shrink to their SHORTEST of the day. In the late afternoon the Sun sinks westward: shadows lengthen again, now pointing east. Ancient people planted a stick in a courtyard — a sundial — and read the time from its shadow for thousands of years!

    Sun LOW (early morning, late afternoon):LONG shadows, gentle light, cooler air.
    Sun HIGH (midday):SHORTEST shadows, strongest sunshine — wear a hat!

    4Why do sunrise and sunset times change with the seasons?

    Join lesson 6.2 with this one: in summer your hemisphere leans TOWARDS the Sun → the Sun rises EARLIER and sets LATER — long days (Hanoi in late June: ~13.5 hours of daylight). Winter flips it: late sunrise, early sunset — short days (~10.5 hours). And the glorious red-orange of dawn and dusk? When the Sun sits near the horizon, its light must cross a much THICKER slice of air; the air scatters the blue light away, letting mostly red-orange reach your eyes. The science behind the most beautiful photos!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna wants to photograph a sea sunrise in Nha Trang and a sunset over the rice fields. Which direction should she point her camera for each photo, and at what time of day should she arrive?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which direction does the Sun always rise in, and set in?
    2. Does sunrise happen at the start or the end of the day?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: For the sunrise — point the camera EAST (Nha Trang's sea faces east, how convenient!) and arrive before dawn. For the sunset — point WEST and arrive in the late afternoon. The rule never changes: rises in the east, sets in the west.
    Example 2

    In the chalk experiment, Nyna's shadow at 8 a.m. was 2 metres long, but at 12 noon only 0.4 metres. Explain why — and predict her shadow at 5 p.m.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What does a low Sun do to shadows? A high Sun?
    2. At 5 p.m., is the Sun high or low?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: At 8 a.m. the Sun is LOW near the eastern horizon — slanted light casts a 2 m shadow stretching west. By noon the Sun stands HIGHEST — nearly vertical light shrinks the shadow to 0.4 m. At 5 p.m. the Sun is LOW again but in the west: the shadow will be LONG again (around 2 m or more), now pointing EAST.
    Example 3

    Nyna's little brother says: "At night the Sun switches off to sleep." Using a globe and a torch, design a 30-second demonstration proving what really happens at night.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Shine the torch steadily at the globe: which half is lit, which is dark?
    2. Slowly spin the globe: stick a paper marker on Vietnam and watch where it travels.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Keep the torch shining STEADILY (the Sun never switches off!). Stick the marker on Vietnam and spin the globe slowly: as the marker turns into the lit half — sunrise, daytime; as it turns on into the dark half — sunset, night. Conclusion for little brother: the Sun burns on always; the Earth's spin simply carries our home to the hidden side — while children on the other half of the globe are greeting their sunrise!

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is adaptation?

    Why do fish never drown, cacti never thirst, and polar bears never shiver? Because every species carries adaptations — special features that help it survive in its habitat. Lesson 6.2 showed how the tilted Earth creates all kinds of climate: hot, cold, wet, dry. Each environment is a different exam question — and each living thing is a beautiful answer to the question of the place it lives. The key skill of this lesson: see a feature, then ask "what JOB does it do THERE?"

    2Hot-land specialists: the camel and the cactus

    The desert sets the exam: scorching sun, scarce water, burning sand. The camel answers with a whole collection of adaptations: a hump storing FAT (a food reserve — not water!), double rows of thick eyelashes against sandstorms, wide pancake feet that never sink in, and the ability to drink 100 litres in one visit. The cactus is the plant champion: a fat juicy stem STORES water, leaves shrunk into SPINES so water cannot evaporate and thirsty raiders keep away, and shallow wide-spreading roots that grab every drop of rare rain.

    3Cold-land and underwater specialists

    The polar regions set the opposite exam: bone-deep cold. The polar bear answers: two thick fur layers (fun truth: the hairs are transparent and the skin beneath is BLACK to soak up sunshine!), an insulating layer of blubber, and wide furry paws for walking on ice. Whales and seals rely on blubber too. Underwater, the exam question is: how to breathe? Fish answer with gills — filtering dissolved air out of the water; streamlined bodies and fins help them glide (remember water resistance from lesson 5.4?). Frogs play both fields: tadpoles breathe with gills underwater, adult frogs climb ashore and breathe with lungs and skin!

    HOT lands call for:Storing water, stopping water loss, dumping heat — humps, spines, big ears.
    COLD lands call for:Keeping heat in — thick fur, blubber, compact round bodies.

    4Body adaptations and behaviour adaptations

    Not every adaptation is a body part! Scientists split them into two groups. Group one: BODY adaptations — things an animal HAS: gills, thick fur, sharp spines, a gecko's sticky toes. Group two: behaviour adaptations — things an animal DOES: storks flying south to escape winter (migration), bears sleeping through the cold months (hibernation), buffalo wallowing in cool mud, owls hunting only at night. Even plants "act": sunflowers turn to follow the Sun, and bàng trees drop their leaves in winter to save water. Body + behaviour = the complete survival toolkit!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Match each feature to its job: (a) a fish's gills; (b) cactus spines; (c) a whale's blubber; (d) a camel's double eyelashes. Jobs: blocking sandstorms / breathing underwater / keeping warm / cutting water loss and deterring eaters.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Ask the key question for each: what JOB does it do THERE?
    2. Think of each environment's exam: water, desert, cold seas.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) gills → breathing underwater; (b) cactus spines → cutting water loss and deterring eaters; (c) whale blubber → keeping warm in cold seas; (d) camel's double lashes → blocking desert sandstorms.
    Example 2

    Sort into BODY or BEHAVIOUR adaptations: (a) a gecko's sticky toes; (b) storks flying south each winter; (c) buffalo wallowing in mud on hot days; (d) a polar bear's transparent fur.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Something the animal HAS = body. Something it DOES = behaviour.
    2. Are flying and wallowing actions or parts?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: BODY — (a) sticky toes (a part it has) and (d) transparent fur. BEHAVIOUR — (b) migrating south (an action it does) and (c) mud-wallowing. Memory trick: HAS = body, DOES = behaviour.
    Example 3

    Thought-experiment question: if a polar bear were moved to a hot desert, what troubles would it face? Name at least TWO features that were superpowers in the Arctic but become burdens there.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What does a superb heat-keeping suit do in 45-degree heat?
    2. Is the bear's usual food (seals) found in a desert?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) The double fur coat + blubber layer — perfect in the Arctic — would dangerously overheat the bear in a desert. (2) Food supply: the bear is a specialist seal-hunter on ice; a desert has neither ice nor seals. (Extra: wide ice-walking paws are wrong for scorching sand.) The big lesson: an adaptation is only a superpower IN ITS OWN PLACE — every living thing is the answer to one specific exam.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The hunter and the hunted

    In nature, one animal's dinner is another animal's great escape. A predator is an animal that hunts others for food: tigers, owls, snakes, even the family cat. Prey is the animal being hunted: mice, rabbits, gazelles, sparrows. The last lesson said every environment sets an exam — for prey, the exam IS the predator; for the predator, the exam is a dinner that runs away! Each side sets the other's test, generation after generation, driving nature's most spectacular adaptation race. Note: one animal can play BOTH parts — a sparrow hunts worms, yet is hunted by cats.

    2The predator's toolkit

    A good hunter needs top equipment: sharp fangs to hold and tear; hook-curved claws to grip; FORWARD-FACING EYES — both eyes aimed at one point to judge the pouncing distance precisely; speed — the cheetah sprints past 100 km/h; and SILENCE: a cat's velvet paw pads, an owl's fringed feathers that erase the sound of wind. Many hunters even borrow the prey's own weapon: camouflage — a tiger's stripes dissolve into tall grass so it can stalk unseen to striking range.

    3The prey's toolkit

    Prey answer back with an equally cunning toolkit. Camouflage: stick insects impersonate twigs, flounders repaint themselves to match the seabed. EYES ON THE SIDES of the head: pigeons and rabbits see almost all the way around, spotting danger early. Escape by speed and zigzag running. Living in a herd: a hundred eyes keep watch, and a hunter struggles to pick one target from a swirling crowd. Warning colours: poison frogs and wasps wear brilliant colours shouting "eat me and regret it!". And the strange tricks: geckos snap off their own tails as decoys, and opossums… play dead!

    PREDATORS often have:Forward eyes · fangs and claws · speed · silent stalking.
    PREY often have:Side eyes · camouflage · herds · warning colours · fast escapes.

    4The arms race — and nature's balance

    A faster hunter → only the fastest, sharpest prey survive to have young → the next prey generation is harder to catch → hunters must improve again… That spiral is nature's "arms race", and it sharpens BOTH sides over millions of years. The final surprise: predators are not the "bad guys"! They keep prey herds healthy (catching the weak and sick first) and keep numbers balanced — without owls and snakes, mice would flood the fields and strip the rice clean. Hunter and hunted hold the web of life steady, together.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Faces only: an owl's eyes aim straight ahead, a pigeon's eyes sit on the sides of its head. Deduce which is hunter and which is hunted — and explain why each eye style suits its role.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What can two eyes aimed at one point measure?
    2. How wide can side-eyes see — and what for?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: The owl is the HUNTER — forward eyes let both eyes lock onto one target, measuring the strike distance precisely even at night. The pigeon is the HUNTED — side eyes sweep almost a full circle, catching cats or hawks sneaking in from any side. The face rule: eyes in front — built to chase; eyes on the side — built to evade!
    Example 2

    Both the TIGER (a predator) and the STICK INSECT (prey) use camouflage. Same trick — how are the two purposes different? State what each uses camouflage FOR.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. How CLOSE must a tiger get before its pounce?
    2. Who must NOT see the stick insect?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: The tiger camouflages to ATTACK — its stripes dissolve into tall grass so it can stalk within pouncing range unseen, because a tiger's sprint only works up close. The stick insect camouflages to DEFEND — impersonating a twig so hunting birds scan past without spotting a meal. One trick, two tactics: hiding to approach, and hiding to be overlooked.
    Example 3

    Most prey try to HIDE, yet the poison dart frog wears BRILLIANT red-and-blue in plain sight. Is that not suicide? Explain this upside-down strategy — and say why wasps chose it too.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. What happens to a predator that once tried eating a poison frog?
    2. What will it do the NEXT time it sees those colours?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Those are WARNING colours — the opposite strategy to camouflage. The frog really IS poisonous, so it does not need to hide; it needs predators to REMEMBER it! A hunter that samples one gets badly sick and learns for life: "brilliant colours = regret". The bolder the display, the harder the lesson is to forget — colour becomes a shield. Wasps did the same: yellow-black stripes announce "I sting". The rule: hide when harmless, advertise when armed!

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Volume
    Độ to

    Volume is how loud or quiet a sound is.

    Volume (Độ to) là mức âm thanh to hay nhỏ.

    Loud
    To

    Thunder is so loud you can hear it kilometres away.

    Sấm Loud (To) đến mức con nghe được từ cách xa nhiều km.

    Quiet
    Nhỏ

    A library stays quiet so everyone can read.

    Thư viện luôn Quiet (Yên tĩnh) để mọi người đọc sách.

    Decibel
    Đề-xi-ben

    Scientists measure volume in decibels (dB) — a whisper is about 20 dB.

    Nhà khoa học đo độ to bằng Decibel (Đề-xi-ben, dB) — tiếng thì thầm khoảng 20 dB.

    Amplitude
    Biên độ

    A bigger amplitude — a taller wave — means a louder sound.

    Amplitude (Biên độ) lớn hơn — sóng cao hơn — nghĩa là âm thanh to hơn.

    Sound meter
    Máy đo âm

    A sound meter shows the decibel level on its screen.

    Sound meter (Máy đo âm) hiển thị mức đề-xi-ben trên màn hình.

    Noise
    Tiếng ồn

    Traffic noise in big cities can reach 85 decibels.

    Noise (Tiếng ồn) giao thông ở thành phố lớn có thể chạm 85 đề-xi-ben.

    Hearing
    Thính giác

    Loud music above 85 dB can slowly damage your hearing.

    Nhạc to trên 85 dB có thể từ từ làm hỏng Hearing (Thính giác) của con.

    Whisper
    Thì thầm

    A whisper measures only about 20 decibels.

    Một tiếng Whisper (Thì thầm) chỉ khoảng 20 đề-xi-ben.

    Roar
    Gầm

    A lion's roar can top 110 decibels — louder than a chainsaw!

    Tiếng Roar (Gầm) của sư tử có thể vượt 110 đề-xi-ben — to hơn cả máy cưa!

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Pitch
    Cao độ

    Pitch is how high or low a sound is.

    Pitch (Cao độ) là mức âm thanh cao hay thấp.

    High
    Cao

    A bird's chirp is a high sound made by fast vibrations.

    Tiếng chim hót là âm High (Cao), do rung động nhanh tạo ra.

    Low
    Thấp

    A big drum makes a low sound from slow vibrations.

    Trống lớn tạo âm Low (Thấp) từ những rung động chậm.

    Frequency
    Tần số

    Frequency counts how many vibrations happen every second.

    Frequency (Tần số) đếm số rung động xảy ra mỗi giây.

    Hertz
    Héc

    Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz) — 440 Hz means 440 vibrations a second.

    Tần số đo bằng Hertz (Héc, Hz) — 440 Hz nghĩa là 440 rung động mỗi giây.

    Fast
    Nhanh

    Fast vibrations make high-pitched sounds.

    Rung động Fast (Nhanh) tạo âm cao.

    Slow
    Chậm

    Slow vibrations make deep, low-pitched sounds.

    Rung động Slow (Chậm) tạo âm trầm, thấp.

    Squeak
    Tiếng rít

    A mouse's squeak is tiny but very high-pitched.

    Squeak (Tiếng rít) của chuột nhỏ xíu nhưng cao vút.

    Rumble
    Tiếng ầm ầm

    Distant thunder is a deep, low rumble.

    Sấm xa là một Rumble (Tiếng ầm ầm) trầm và thấp.

    Note
    Nốt nhạc

    Each piano key plays a note with its own exact frequency.

    Mỗi phím đàn piano chơi một Note (Nốt nhạc) với tần số chính xác riêng.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Force
    Lực

    More force on the drum means a bigger vibration and a louder boom.

    Nhiều Force (Lực) hơn lên mặt trống nghĩa là rung lớn hơn và tiếng «tùng» to hơn.

    Harder
    Mạnh hơn

    Strike the xylophone harder and the note gets louder.

    Gõ đàn phiến gỗ Harder (Mạnh hơn) và nốt nhạc to lên.

    Softer
    Nhẹ hơn

    Pluck the string softer to play a quieter note.

    Gảy dây Softer (Nhẹ hơn) để chơi nốt nhỏ hơn.

    Energy
    Năng lượng

    A loud sound carries more energy than a quiet one.

    Âm thanh to mang nhiều Energy (Năng lượng) hơn âm thanh nhỏ.

    Muffle
    Làm nghẹt tiếng

    A thick blanket over the speaker muffles the music.

    Tấm chăn dày phủ lên loa Muffle (Làm nghẹt) tiếng nhạc.

    Absorb
    Hấp thụ

    Soft materials like foam absorb sound instead of bouncing it back.

    Vật liệu mềm như mút xốp Absorb (Hấp thụ) âm thanh thay vì dội lại.

    Insulation
    Cách âm

    Studios use thick wall insulation to keep sound in and noise out.

    Phòng thu dùng lớp Insulation (Cách âm) dày để giữ âm bên trong và chặn ồn bên ngoài.

    Distance
    Khoảng cách

    Volume drops as the distance from the source grows.

    Độ to giảm dần khi Distance (Khoảng cách) tới nguồn âm tăng lên.

    Megaphone
    Loa cầm tay

    A megaphone funnels sound one way, making the voice louder ahead.

    Megaphone (Loa cầm tay) dồn âm thanh về một hướng, làm giọng nói to hơn ở phía trước.

    Earmuffs
    Chụp tai

    Builders wear earmuffs to protect their hearing from loud machines.

    Thợ xây đeo Earmuffs (Chụp tai) để bảo vệ thính giác khỏi máy móc ồn ào.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    String
    Dây đàn

    Each guitar string plays a different pitch.

    Mỗi String (Dây đàn) guitar chơi một cao độ khác nhau.

    Length
    Chiều dài

    Shorter length means faster vibration and higher pitch.

    Length (Chiều dài) ngắn hơn nghĩa là rung nhanh hơn và âm cao hơn.

    Tight
    Căng

    Turning the tuning peg makes the string tighter and the note higher.

    Vặn khoá đàn làm dây Tight (Căng) hơn và nốt cao hơn.

    Loose
    Chùng

    A loose string vibrates slowly and plays a low note.

    Dây Loose (Chùng) rung chậm và chơi nốt thấp.

    Thick
    Dày

    The thick strings on a guitar play the lowest notes.

    Những dây Thick (Dày) trên đàn guitar chơi các nốt thấp nhất.

    Thin
    Mảnh

    Thin strings vibrate fast and sound high.

    Dây Thin (Mảnh) rung nhanh và kêu cao.

    Air column
    Cột không khí

    Blowing across a bottle makes the air column inside vibrate.

    Thổi ngang miệng chai làm Air column (Cột không khí) bên trong rung lên.

    Shorten
    Rút ngắn

    Pressing a guitar fret shortens the string and raises the pitch.

    Bấm phím đàn guitar Shorten (Rút ngắn) sợi dây và nâng cao độ lên.

    Tune
    Chỉnh dây

    Musicians tune their instruments by adjusting string tightness.

    Nhạc công Tune (Chỉnh dây) nhạc cụ bằng cách điều chỉnh độ căng của dây.

    Instrument
    Nhạc cụ

    Every instrument changes pitch in its own clever way.

    Mỗi Instrument (Nhạc cụ) thay đổi cao độ theo cách khéo léo riêng.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Matter
    Vật chất

    Everything you can touch — air included — is made of matter.

    Mọi thứ con chạm được — kể cả không khí — đều làm từ Matter (Vật chất).

    Particle
    Hạt

    All matter is built from particles too small to see.

    Mọi vật chất được xây từ các Particle (Hạt) nhỏ đến mức không nhìn thấy.

    Solid
    Chất rắn

    In a solid, particles hold hands in neat rows and only wiggle.

    Trong Solid (Chất rắn), các hạt nắm tay nhau thành hàng ngay ngắn và chỉ rung nhẹ.

    Liquid
    Chất lỏng

    A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

    Liquid (Chất lỏng) chảy được và mang hình dạng của vật chứa nó.

    Gas
    Chất khí

    A gas spreads out to fill every corner of its container.

    Gas (Chất khí) lan ra lấp đầy mọi ngóc ngách của vật chứa.

    Flow
    Chảy

    Liquids and gases can flow; solids cannot.

    Chất lỏng và chất khí có thể Flow (Chảy); chất rắn thì không.

    Container
    Vật chứa

    A gas fills its whole container, whatever the shape.

    Chất khí lấp đầy toàn bộ Container (Vật chứa), bất kể hình dạng gì.

    Compress
    Nén

    You can compress a gas — squeeze its particles closer together.

    Con có thể Compress (Nén) chất khí — ép các hạt của nó sát lại nhau.

    Spread
    Lan toả

    Perfume particles spread across the room in minutes.

    Các hạt nước hoa Spread (Lan toả) khắp phòng trong vài phút.

    Model
    Mô hình

    The particle model helps scientists explain how matter behaves.

    Model (Mô hình) hạt giúp nhà khoa học giải thích cách vật chất hành xử.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Temperature
    Nhiệt độ

    Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is.

    Temperature (Nhiệt độ) cho biết một vật nóng hay lạnh đến đâu.

    Thermometer
    Nhiệt kế

    A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius.

    Thermometer (Nhiệt kế) đo nhiệt độ theo độ C.

    Celsius
    Độ C

    On the Celsius scale, water freezes at 0° and boils at 100°.

    Trên thang Celsius (Độ C), nước đóng băng ở 0° và sôi ở 100°.

    Melt
    Tan chảy

    Ice melts into liquid water when it warms above 0°C.

    Nước đá Melt (Tan chảy) thành nước lỏng khi ấm lên trên 0°C.

    Melting point
    Điểm nóng chảy

    Water's melting point is 0°C — ice cannot stay frozen above it.

    Melting point (Điểm nóng chảy) của nước là 0°C — trên mức đó đá không thể đông được.

    Boil
    Sôi

    Water boils fiercely, bubbling as it turns to gas.

    Nước Boil (Sôi) sùng sục, nổi bong bóng khi hoá thành hơi.

    Boiling point
    Điểm sôi

    At sea level, water's boiling point is 100°C.

    Ở ngang mực nước biển, Boiling point (Điểm sôi) của nước là 100°C.

    Freeze
    Đóng băng

    Water freezes solid at 0°C.

    Nước Freeze (Đóng băng) thành thể rắn ở 0°C.

    Ice
    Nước đá

    Ice is solid water — and strangely, it floats on liquid water.

    Ice (Nước đá) là nước ở thể rắn — và kỳ lạ thay, nó nổi trên nước lỏng.

    Steam
    Hơi nước

    Steam rises from boiling water — water in its gas state.

    Steam (Hơi nước) bốc lên từ nước sôi — nước ở thể khí.

    Evaporation
    Sự bay hơi

    Evaporation turns puddle water into invisible vapour, even without boiling.

    Evaporation (Sự bay hơi) biến nước vũng thành hơi vô hình, không cần sôi.

    Condensation
    Sự ngưng tụ

    Condensation paints water droplets on a cold glass of juice.

    Condensation (Sự ngưng tụ) vẽ những giọt nước lên ly nước trái cây lạnh.

    Water vapour
    Hơi nước

    Invisible water vapour is always floating in the air around you.

    Water vapour (Hơi nước) vô hình luôn lơ lửng trong không khí quanh con.

    Water cycle
    Vòng tuần hoàn nước

    The water cycle loops forever: evaporate, condense, rain, repeat.

    Water cycle (Vòng tuần hoàn nước) quay mãi: bay hơi, ngưng tụ, mưa, lặp lại.

    Cloud
    Đám mây

    A cloud is billions of tiny condensed water droplets floating together.

    Cloud (Đám mây) là hàng tỷ giọt nước li ti ngưng tụ trôi cùng nhau.

    Precipitation
    Giáng thuỷ

    Rain, snow and hail are all kinds of precipitation.

    Mưa, tuyết và mưa đá đều là các dạng Precipitation (Giáng thuỷ).

    Puddle
    Vũng nước

    After rain, puddles shrink hour by hour as they evaporate.

    Sau cơn mưa, các Puddle (Vũng nước) nhỏ dần từng giờ vì bay hơi.

    Dew
    Sương

    Morning dew is vapour that condensed on cool grass overnight.

    Dew (Sương) buổi sớm là hơi nước ngưng tụ trên cỏ mát suốt đêm.

    Surface
    Bề mặt

    Evaporation happens at the liquid's surface, where particles can escape.

    Sự bay hơi xảy ra ở Surface (Bề mặt) chất lỏng, nơi các hạt thoát ra được.

    Dry
    Khô

    Wet clothes dry fastest on hot, windy days.

    Quần áo ướt Dry (Khô) nhanh nhất vào ngày nóng và lộng gió.

    Solution
    Dung dịch

    Sugar stirred into tea makes a sweet solution.

    Đường khuấy vào trà tạo thành một Solution (Dung dịch) ngọt.

    Dissolve
    Hoà tan

    Salt seems to vanish when it dissolves in water — but it is still there.

    Muối như biến mất khi Dissolve (Hoà tan) trong nước — nhưng nó vẫn ở đó.

    Solute
    Chất tan

    In salt water, salt is the solute — the thing that dissolves.

    Trong nước muối, muối là Solute (Chất tan) — thứ được hoà tan.

    Solvent
    Dung môi

    Water is the world's best solvent — it dissolves more things than any other liquid.

    Nước là Solvent (Dung môi) giỏi nhất thế giới — hoà tan nhiều chất hơn mọi chất lỏng khác.

    Mixture
    Hỗn hợp

    Sand in water is a mixture — the sand never dissolves.

    Cát trong nước là một Mixture (Hỗn hợp) — cát không bao giờ tan.

    Soluble
    Tan được

    Sugar and salt are soluble in water.

    Đường và muối Soluble (Tan được) trong nước.

    Insoluble
    Không tan

    Sand and chalk are insoluble — stir all day, they will not dissolve.

    Cát và phấn Insoluble (Không tan) — khuấy cả ngày cũng không tan.

    Stir
    Khuấy

    Stirring helps the solute spread and dissolve faster.

    Stir (Khuấy) giúp chất tan lan ra và hoà tan nhanh hơn.

    Filter
    Lọc

    A filter catches insoluble bits but lets the solution pass through.

    Filter (Lọc) giữ lại phần không tan nhưng cho dung dịch đi qua.

    Transparent
    Trong suốt

    A true solution is transparent — you can see right through it.

    Dung dịch thật sự thì Transparent (Trong suốt) — con nhìn xuyên qua được.

    Digestion
    Sự tiêu hoá

    Digestion is the journey that turns food into fuel for your body.

    Digestion (Sự tiêu hoá) là hành trình biến thức ăn thành nhiên liệu cho cơ thể.

    Mouth
    Miệng

    The journey starts in the mouth, where teeth chop and saliva softens.

    Hành trình bắt đầu ở Mouth (Miệng), nơi răng nghiền và nước bọt làm mềm thức ăn.

    Teeth
    Răng

    Teeth cut and grind food into small, easy pieces.

    Teeth (Răng) cắt và nghiền thức ăn thành những mẩu nhỏ dễ nuốt.

    Tongue
    Lưỡi

    The tongue mixes food and pushes it back to be swallowed.

    Tongue (Lưỡi) trộn thức ăn và đẩy nó ra sau để nuốt xuống.

    Saliva
    Nước bọt

    Saliva wets food and starts breaking it down before you even swallow.

    Saliva (Nước bọt) làm ướt thức ăn và bắt đầu phân giải nó trước cả khi con nuốt.

    Oesophagus
    Thực quản

    The oesophagus is the food pipe squeezing each bite down to the stomach.

    Oesophagus (Thực quản) là ống dẫn bóp từng miếng thức ăn xuống dạ dày.

    Stomach
    Dạ dày

    The stomach churns food with strong acid like a washing machine.

    Stomach (Dạ dày) nhào trộn thức ăn với axit mạnh như chiếc máy giặt.

    Small intestine
    Ruột non

    The small intestine is a 6-metre tube where nutrients enter the blood.

    Small intestine (Ruột non) là ống dài 6 mét, nơi chất dinh dưỡng đi vào máu.

    Large intestine
    Ruột già

    The large intestine reclaims water and packs up the leftovers.

    Large intestine (Ruột già) thu hồi nước và đóng gói phần thừa.

    Organ
    Cơ quan

    Each organ of the system has its own special job.

    Mỗi Organ (Cơ quan) trong hệ thống có nhiệm vụ riêng của mình.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Nutrient
    Chất dinh dưỡng

    Nutrients are the useful parts of food that your body keeps.

    Nutrient (Chất dinh dưỡng) là phần hữu ích của thức ăn mà cơ thể giữ lại.

    Break down
    Phân giải

    Digestion breaks down big food pieces into tiny useful bits.

    Tiêu hoá Break down (Phân giải) các mẩu thức ăn to thành những mảnh nhỏ hữu ích.

    Churn
    Nhào trộn

    The stomach churns food like a slow, strong mixer.

    Dạ dày Churn (Nhào trộn) thức ăn như chiếc máy trộn chậm mà khoẻ.

    Peristalsis
    Nhu động

    Peristalsis is the muscle wave that pushes food along the tube.

    Peristalsis (Nhu động) là đợt sóng cơ đẩy thức ăn dọc theo đường ống.

    Enzyme
    Enzym

    Enzymes are chemical scissors that snip food into tiny pieces.

    Enzyme (Enzym) là những chiếc kéo hoá học cắt thức ăn thành mảnh li ti.

    Acid
    Axit

    Stomach acid dissolves food and kills germs that ride in with it.

    Acid (Axit) dạ dày hoà tan thức ăn và diệt vi trùng đi kèm theo nó.

    Mucus
    Chất nhầy

    A layer of mucus shields the stomach from its own acid.

    Một lớp Mucus (Chất nhầy) che chắn dạ dày khỏi chính axit của nó.

    Blood
    Máu

    Nutrients travel in the blood to every cell of the body.

    Chất dinh dưỡng theo Blood (Máu) đến từng tế bào của cơ thể.

    Waste
    Chất thải

    The parts of food the body cannot use leave as waste.

    Phần thức ăn cơ thể không dùng được sẽ rời đi dưới dạng Waste (Chất thải).

    Fuel
    Nhiên liệu

    Food is the body's fuel — it powers running, thinking and growing.

    Thức ăn là Fuel (Nhiên liệu) của cơ thể — cung cấp sức cho chạy nhảy, suy nghĩ và lớn lên.

    Balanced diet
    Chế độ ăn cân bằng

    A balanced diet gives your body a bit of everything it needs.

    Balanced diet (Chế độ ăn cân bằng) cho cơ thể một chút của mọi thứ nó cần.

    Portion
    Khẩu phần

    Doctors suggest five portions of fruit and vegetables a day.

    Bác sĩ khuyên năm Portion (Khẩu phần) rau quả mỗi ngày.

    Variety
    Sự đa dạng

    Variety matters — different foods bring different nutrients.

    Variety (Sự đa dạng) rất quan trọng — mỗi món mang chất dinh dưỡng khác nhau.

    Vitamin
    Vitamin

    Vitamins are tiny helpers your body cannot make enough of itself.

    Vitamin là những trợ thủ tí hon mà cơ thể không tự tạo đủ.

    Mineral
    Khoáng chất

    Minerals like calcium build strong bones and teeth.

    Mineral (Khoáng chất) như canxi xây xương và răng chắc khoẻ.

    Fibre
    Chất xơ

    Fibre from vegetables keeps your digestion running smoothly.

    Fibre (Chất xơ) từ rau củ giữ hệ tiêu hoá chạy trơn tru.

    Healthy
    Lành mạnh

    A healthy plate is colourful — greens, reds, yellows and more.

    Một đĩa ăn Healthy (Lành mạnh) thì đầy màu sắc — xanh, đỏ, vàng và hơn thế.

    Junk food
    Đồ ăn vặt

    Junk food tastes fun but gives little besides sugar and fat.

    Junk food (Đồ ăn vặt) ăn vui miệng nhưng cho ít thứ ngoài đường và mỡ.

    Meal
    Bữa ăn

    Three balanced meals a day keep your energy steady.

    Ba Meal (Bữa ăn) cân bằng mỗi ngày giữ năng lượng của con ổn định.

    Snack
    Bữa phụ

    A fruit snack beats a candy snack between meals.

    Snack (Bữa phụ) bằng trái cây tốt hơn kẹo ngọt giữa các bữa chính.

    Food group
    Nhóm thực phẩm

    Foods with similar nutrients belong to the same food group.

    Thức ăn có dinh dưỡng giống nhau thuộc cùng một Food group (Nhóm thực phẩm).

    Carbohydrate
    Chất bột đường

    Carbohydrates in rice and bread are the body's main energy source.

    Carbohydrate (Chất bột đường) trong cơm và bánh mì là nguồn năng lượng chính của cơ thể.

    Protein
    Chất đạm

    Protein from fish, eggs and beans builds and repairs your body.

    Protein (Chất đạm) từ cá, trứng và đậu xây dựng và sửa chữa cơ thể con.

    Fat
    Chất béo

    A little healthy fat keeps your brain and skin working well.

    Một chút Fat (Chất béo) lành mạnh giúp não và da hoạt động tốt.

    Sugar
    Đường

    Sugar is a fast carbohydrate — quick energy that burns out quickly.

    Sugar (Đường) là chất bột đường nhanh — năng lượng tức thì nhưng chóng tàn.

    Starch
    Tinh bột

    Starch in rice and potatoes releases energy slowly and steadily.

    Starch (Tinh bột) trong cơm và khoai giải phóng năng lượng chậm và đều.

    Dairy
    Chế phẩm sữa

    Dairy foods like milk, cheese and yogurt are rich in calcium.

    Dairy (Chế phẩm sữa) như sữa, phô mai, sữa chua rất giàu canxi.

    Grain
    Ngũ cốc

    Rice, wheat and corn are grains — seeds of grass plants.

    Gạo, lúa mì và ngô là Grain (Ngũ cốc) — hạt của các cây họ cỏ.

    Calcium
    Canxi

    Calcium from dairy builds strong bones and teeth.

    Calcium (Canxi) từ sữa xây xương và răng chắc khoẻ.

    Iron
    Chất sắt

    Iron in meat and dark greens helps blood carry oxygen.

    Iron (Chất sắt) trong thịt và rau xanh đậm giúp máu chở ôxy.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Force
    Lực

    A force is a push or a pull acting on an object.

    Force (Lực) là một cú đẩy hoặc kéo tác động lên vật.

    Push
    Đẩy

    You push a swing to send it away from you.

    Con Push (Đẩy) chiếc xích đu để nó rời xa mình.

    Pull
    Kéo

    You pull a wagon to bring it towards you.

    Con Pull (Kéo) chiếc xe để đưa nó về phía mình.

    Gravity
    Trọng lực

    Gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth.

    Gravity (Trọng lực) kéo mọi vật về phía tâm Trái Đất.

    Friction
    Ma sát

    Friction between shoes and floor stops you from slipping.

    Friction (Ma sát) giữa giày và sàn giúp con không trượt ngã.

    Air resistance
    Lực cản không khí

    Air resistance slows a falling parachute.

    Air resistance (Lực cản không khí) làm chậm chiếc dù đang rơi.

    Upthrust
    Lực đẩy nổi

    Upthrust from the water keeps a boat floating.

    Upthrust (Lực đẩy nổi) từ nước giữ con thuyền nổi trên mặt.

    Newton
    Niu-tơn

    Forces are measured in newtons (N), named after Isaac Newton.

    Lực được đo bằng Newton (Niu-tơn, N), đặt theo tên Isaac Newton.

    Weight
    Trọng lượng

    Weight is the force of gravity pulling on your body.

    Weight (Trọng lượng) là lực trọng trường kéo lên cơ thể con.

    Motion
    Chuyển động

    Forces can start, stop or change an object's motion.

    Lực có thể khởi động, dừng lại hay thay đổi Motion (Chuyển động) của vật.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Diagram
    Sơ đồ

    A force diagram shows all the forces acting on one object.

    Diagram (Sơ đồ) lực thể hiện mọi lực đang tác động lên một vật.

    Arrow
    Mũi tên

    Each arrow in the diagram stands for one force.

    Mỗi Arrow (Mũi tên) trong sơ đồ đại diện cho một lực.

    Direction
    Hướng

    The arrow points in the direction the force acts.

    Mũi tên chỉ theo Direction (Hướng) mà lực tác động.

    Size
    Độ lớn

    A longer arrow means a bigger force size.

    Mũi tên dài hơn nghĩa là Size (Độ lớn) của lực to hơn.

    Label
    Nhãn

    Label each arrow with the force's name and its newtons.

    Hãy ghi Label (Nhãn) cho mỗi mũi tên với tên lực và số niu-tơn.

    Act
    Tác động

    Several forces can act on one object at the same time.

    Nhiều lực có thể Act (Tác động) lên một vật cùng lúc.

    Balanced
    Cân bằng

    Balanced forces cancel out — the object's motion stays unchanged.

    Các lực Balanced (Cân bằng) triệt tiêu nhau — chuyển động của vật không đổi.

    Unbalanced
    Không cân bằng

    Unbalanced forces make the object speed up, slow down or turn.

    Lực Unbalanced (Không cân bằng) làm vật tăng tốc, chậm lại hoặc đổi hướng.

    Resultant
    Hợp lực

    The resultant is the one force left after adding all the others.

    Resultant (Hợp lực) là lực duy nhất còn lại sau khi cộng tất cả các lực.

    Measure
    Đo

    A force meter measures forces in newtons.

    Lực kế Measure (Đo) các lực theo đơn vị niu-tơn.

    Satellite
    Vệ tinh

    A satellite is anything that orbits a planet.

    Satellite (Vệ tinh) là bất cứ thứ gì quay quanh một hành tinh.

    Orbit
    Quỹ đạo

    The Moon takes about a month to complete one orbit of Earth.

    Mặt Trăng mất khoảng một tháng để đi hết một Orbit (Quỹ đạo) quanh Trái Đất.

    Moon
    Mặt Trăng

    The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.

    Moon (Mặt Trăng) là vệ tinh tự nhiên duy nhất của Trái Đất.

    Natural
    Tự nhiên

    A natural satellite is made by nature, not by people.

    Vệ tinh Natural (Tự nhiên) do thiên nhiên tạo ra, không phải con người.

    Artificial
    Nhân tạo

    Artificial satellites are machines built and launched by people.

    Vệ tinh Artificial (Nhân tạo) là máy móc do con người chế tạo và phóng lên.

    Planet
    Hành tinh

    Every planet with a moon has at least one natural satellite.

    Mỗi Planet (Hành tinh) có mặt trăng đều có ít nhất một vệ tinh tự nhiên.

    Spacecraft
    Tàu vũ trụ

    A spacecraft carried each satellite up into space.

    Một Spacecraft (Tàu vũ trụ) đã đưa từng vệ tinh lên không gian.

    Signal
    Tín hiệu

    TV and phone signals bounce off satellites high above us.

    Signal (Tín hiệu) truyền hình và điện thoại dội qua các vệ tinh cao trên đầu ta.

    Astronaut
    Phi hành gia

    Astronauts live aboard the biggest artificial satellite of all.

    Các Astronaut (Phi hành gia) sống trên vệ tinh nhân tạo lớn nhất trong tất cả.

    Space station
    Trạm vũ trụ

    The International Space Station circles Earth every 90 minutes.

    Space station (Trạm vũ trụ) Quốc tế vòng quanh Trái Đất mỗi 90 phút.

    Combine
    Kết hợp

    When several forces combine, we feel only their total effect.

    Khi nhiều lực Combine (Kết hợp), ta chỉ cảm nhận tác dụng tổng của chúng.

    Add
    Cộng

    Forces pushing the SAME way add together.

    Các lực đẩy CÙNG chiều thì Add (Cộng) lại với nhau.

    Subtract
    Trừ

    Forces pulling OPPOSITE ways subtract from each other.

    Các lực kéo NGƯỢC chiều thì Subtract (Trừ) đi lẫn nhau.

    Opposite
    Ngược chiều

    Weight and upthrust act in opposite directions.

    Trọng lượng và lực đẩy nổi tác động theo hai hướng Opposite (Ngược chiều).

    Speed up
    Tăng tốc

    An unbalanced force forward makes a bike speed up.

    Hợp lực hướng về trước làm xe đạp Speed up (Tăng tốc).

    Slow down
    Giảm tốc

    Friction and air resistance make moving things slow down.

    Ma sát và lực cản không khí làm vật chuyển động Slow down (Giảm tốc).

    Change
    Thay đổi

    Only an unbalanced force can change how an object moves.

    Chỉ lực không cân bằng mới Change (Thay đổi) được cách vật chuyển động.

    Float
    Nổi

    An object floats when upthrust can balance its weight.

    Vật Float (Nổi) khi lực đẩy nổi cân bằng được trọng lượng của nó.

    Sink
    Chìm

    An object sinks when its weight beats the upthrust.

    Vật Sink (Chìm) khi trọng lượng của nó thắng lực đẩy nổi.

    Water resistance
    Lực cản của nước

    Water resistance pushes back against every swimmer.

    Water resistance (Lực cản của nước) đẩy ngược lại mọi người bơi.

    Magnet
    Nam châm

    A magnet can pull some metals without touching them.

    Magnet (Nam châm) có thể hút một số kim loại mà không cần chạm vào.

    Magnetic
    Có từ tính

    Iron and steel are magnetic materials.

    Sắt và thép là các vật liệu Magnetic (Có từ tính).

    Pole
    Cực

    Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

    Mỗi nam châm đều có một Pole (Cực) bắc và một cực nam.

    Attract
    Hút

    Opposite poles attract each other.

    Hai cực khác tên Attract (Hút) lẫn nhau.

    Repel
    Đẩy

    Two like poles repel each other.

    Hai cực cùng tên Repel (Đẩy) lẫn nhau.

    Iron
    Sắt

    Iron nails jump to a magnet from a distance.

    Đinh Iron (Sắt) nhảy về phía nam châm từ xa.

    Steel
    Thép

    Steel paper clips stick to magnets because steel contains iron.

    Kẹp giấy Steel (Thép) dính vào nam châm vì thép chứa sắt.

    Compass
    La bàn

    A compass needle is a tiny magnet that points north.

    Kim Compass (La bàn) là một nam châm tí hon luôn chỉ hướng bắc.

    North
    Bắc

    The north pole of a magnet is often painted red.

    Cực North (Bắc) của nam châm thường được sơn đỏ.

    South
    Nam

    A north pole attracts the south pole of another magnet.

    Cực bắc hút cực South (Nam) của nam châm khác.

    Earth
    Trái Đất

    The Earth travels around the Sun without ever stopping.

    Earth (Trái Đất) di chuyển quanh Mặt Trời không bao giờ ngừng nghỉ.

    Sun
    Mặt Trời

    The Sun is the star at the centre of Earth's orbit.

    Sun (Mặt Trời) là ngôi sao ở tâm quỹ đạo của Trái Đất.

    Year
    Năm

    One full trip of Earth around the Sun takes one year.

    Một vòng trọn vẹn của Trái Đất quanh Mặt Trời mất một Year (Năm).

    Rotation
    Sự tự quay

    Earth's rotation on its axis gives us day and night.

    Rotation (Sự tự quay) của Trái Đất quanh trục cho ta ngày và đêm.

    Revolution
    Sự quay quanh

    One revolution around the Sun equals one whole year.

    Một Revolution (Sự quay quanh) Mặt Trời bằng đúng một năm.

    Axis
    Trục

    Earth spins around an invisible line called its axis.

    Trái Đất xoay quanh một đường vô hình gọi là Axis (Trục).

    Spin
    Xoay

    The Earth completes one full spin every 24 hours.

    Trái Đất hoàn thành một vòng Spin (Xoay) trọn vẹn mỗi 24 giờ.

    Day
    Ngày

    One day is the time of one full spin of the Earth.

    Một Day (Ngày) là thời gian một vòng xoay trọn vẹn của Trái Đất.

    Leap year
    Năm nhuận

    A leap year adds one extra day: February the 29th.

    Leap year (Năm nhuận) thêm một ngày phụ: 29 tháng Hai.

    Star
    Ngôi sao

    Our Sun is a star — the only one close enough to feel warm.

    Mặt Trời của ta là một Star (Ngôi sao) — ngôi sao duy nhất đủ gần để ta thấy ấm.

    Tilt (Độ nghiêng) 23,5 độ của Trái Đất cho chúng ta các mùa.

    Season
    Mùa

    Each season brings its own weather and daylight hours.

    Mỗi Season (Mùa) mang theo thời tiết và số giờ nắng riêng.

    Summer
    Mùa hè

    Summer days are long, bright and warm.

    Ngày Summer (Mùa hè) dài, sáng và ấm áp.

    Winter
    Mùa đông

    Winter brings short days and the coldest weather.

    Winter (Mùa đông) mang đến ngày ngắn và thời tiết lạnh nhất.

    Spring
    Mùa xuân

    Flowers bloom and days grow longer in spring.

    Hoa nở và ngày dài dần ra trong Spring (Mùa xuân).

    Autumn
    Mùa thu

    In autumn, leaves turn gold and days grow shorter.

    Vào Autumn (Mùa thu), lá chuyển vàng và ngày ngắn dần.

    Hemisphere
    Bán cầu

    The equator divides Earth into two hemispheres.

    Xích đạo chia Trái Đất thành hai Hemisphere (Bán cầu).

    Equator
    Xích đạo

    Countries near the equator stay warm all year round.

    Các nước gần Equator (Xích đạo) ấm áp quanh năm.

    Sunlight
    Ánh nắng

    The tilted half facing the Sun catches stronger sunlight.

    Nửa nghiêng về phía Mặt Trời hứng Sunlight (Ánh nắng) mạnh hơn.

    Temperature
    Nhiệt độ

    Summer temperatures climb while winter temperatures drop.

    Temperature (Nhiệt độ) mùa hè tăng cao còn mùa đông hạ thấp.

    Sunrise
    Bình minh

    At sunrise, the Sun appears above the horizon in the east.

    Lúc Sunrise (Bình minh), Mặt Trời hiện lên trên đường chân trời phía đông.

    Sunset
    Hoàng hôn

    At sunset, the sky often glows orange and pink.

    Lúc Sunset (Hoàng hôn), bầu trời thường rực cam và hồng.

    East
    Hướng đông

    The Sun always rises in the east.

    Mặt Trời luôn mọc ở East (Hướng đông).

    West
    Hướng tây

    The Sun always sets in the west.

    Mặt Trời luôn lặn ở West (Hướng tây).

    Noon
    Buổi trưa

    At noon the Sun stands highest in the sky.

    Vào Noon (Buổi trưa) Mặt Trời đứng cao nhất trên bầu trời.

    Shadow
    Cái bóng

    Your shadow is longest in the early morning and evening.

    Shadow (Cái bóng) của con dài nhất vào sáng sớm và chiều muộn.

    Horizon
    Đường chân trời

    The Sun seems to sink below the horizon at dusk.

    Mặt Trời như chìm xuống dưới Horizon (Đường chân trời) lúc chạng vạng.

    Apparent
    Biểu kiến

    The Sun's journey across the sky is only apparent motion.

    Hành trình của Mặt Trời ngang bầu trời chỉ là chuyển động Apparent (Biểu kiến).

    Midday
    Giữa trưa

    Midday shadows are the shortest of the whole day.

    Bóng lúc Midday (Giữa trưa) ngắn nhất trong cả ngày.

    Sky
    Bầu trời

    The Sun seems to travel across the sky from east to west.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Adaptation
    Sự thích nghi

    An adaptation is a special feature that helps a living thing survive.

    Adaptation (Sự thích nghi) là đặc điểm riêng giúp sinh vật sống sót.

    Habitat
    Môi trường sống

    A frog's habitat includes both water and land.

    Habitat (Môi trường sống) của ếch gồm cả nước lẫn đất liền.

    Survive
    Sống sót

    Thick fur helps polar bears survive the freezing Arctic.

    Bộ lông dày giúp gấu Bắc Cực Survive (Sống sót) qua giá rét vùng cực.

    Environment
    Môi trường

    Each environment — hot, cold, wet or dry — shapes its animals.

    Mỗi Environment (Môi trường) — nóng, lạnh, ẩm hay khô — đều nhào nặn các loài vật của nó.

    Desert
    Sa mạc

    Camels cross the desert for days without drinking.

    Lạc đà băng qua Desert (Sa mạc) nhiều ngày không cần uống nước.

    Polar
    Vùng cực

    Polar animals wear thick fur coats and layers of fat.

    Động vật Polar (Vùng cực) khoác áo lông dày và các lớp mỡ.

    Feature
    Đặc điểm

    A cactus spine is a feature that guards its water.

    Gai xương rồng là một Feature (Đặc điểm) bảo vệ nguồn nước của nó.

    Behaviour
    Tập tính

    Flying south for winter is a behaviour adaptation of many birds.

    Bay về phương nam tránh rét là Behaviour (Tập tính) thích nghi của nhiều loài chim.

    Blubber
    Mỡ dày

    Whales keep warm with a thick layer of blubber.

    Cá voi giữ ấm nhờ lớp Blubber (Mỡ dày).

    Gills
    Mang cá

    Fish breathe underwater using their gills.

    Cá thở dưới nước nhờ Gills (Mang cá) của chúng.

    Christmas trees

    Pines are conifers — their seeds hide in cones, not flowers

    Damp walls

    The green fuzz on shady walls is moss, spreading by spores

    Shady gardens

    Ferns unroll their feathery leaves where flowers struggle to grow

    Rice paddies

    Rice is a flowering plant — its tiny flowers become the grains we eat

    Glossary

    Flowering plant
    A plant that reproduces using flowers and seeds.
    Non-flowering plant
    A plant that reproduces without flowers, often using spores or cones.
    Spore
    A tiny dust-like cell some plants use instead of seeds.
    Cone
    The woody case where conifer trees keep their seeds.
    Fern
    A non-flowering plant with feathery leaves that makes spores.
    Moss
    A tiny non-flowering plant that grows in soft green mats.
    Conifer
    A tree that makes seeds in cones and usually has needle leaves.
    Reproduce
    To make new living things of the same kind.
    Seed
    A capsule holding a baby plant and its food store.
    Species
    One particular kind of living thing.

    Try it yourself: take a 10-minute plant hunt around your home or street. Find 5 plants and sort them: which ones make flowers, and which never do? Look closely at any ferns or moss — can you spot the spore dots?

    Did you know?

    • An English oak tree does not grow its first acorns until it is about 40 years old.Source: Woodland Trust ↗
    • Bamboo is the fastest-growing plant on Earth — some kinds grow up to 91 cm in a single day.Source: Guinness World Records ↗

    Glossary

    Life cycle
    The repeating stages of a living thing's life.
    Germination
    When a seed starts growing into a plant.
    Seedling
    A very young plant just grown from a seed.
    Mature plant
    A fully grown plant that can reproduce.
    Flower
    The reproduction part of a flowering plant.
    Fruit
    The seed case that grows from a pollinated flower.
    Roots
    The plant parts that grow down, hold the plant and take in water.
    Shoot
    The young stem that grows upward towards light.
    Wilt
    To droop and fade after flowering or without water.
    Stage
    One step in a cycle or process.

    Try it yourself: plant a bean in a clear jar against damp cotton wool. Draw it every 2 days for two weeks. Label each stage you see: seed → germination → root → shoot → seedling. Which appeared first, root or shoot?

    Glossary

    Pollination
    Moving pollen from one flower to another so seeds can form.
    Pollen
    The powder flowers make for reproduction.
    Petal
    The coloured part of a flower that attracts pollinators.
    Stamen
    The male part of a flower that makes pollen.
    Anther
    The pollen-making tip of the stamen.
    Stigma
    The sticky tip of the female part that catches pollen.
    Carpel
    The female part of a flower where seeds begin.
    Nectar
    The sweet drink flowers offer to visiting animals.
    Pollinator
    An animal that carries pollen between flowers.
    Fertilisation
    When pollen joins an egg cell so a seed can grow.

    Try it yourself: watch a flowering bush for 10 minutes on a sunny day. Count the visitors — bees, butterflies, ants, birds. Watch one bee closely: can you see the yellow pollen dust sticking to its fuzzy body?

    Did you know?

    • On a hot summer day you can HEAR gorse bushes popping as their seed pods burst and fling seeds through the air.Source: Woodland Trust ↗
    • Spinning helicopter seeds fly so well that they inspired engineers designing single-bladed aircraft.Source: Woodland Trust ↗
