    Glossary

    Dispersal
    Spreading seeds away from the parent plant.
    Wind
    Moving air that can carry light seeds far away.
    Parachute
    A fluffy tuft that lets a seed drift on the breeze.
    Wing
    A flat blade that makes a falling seed spin and drift.
    Hook
    A tiny curved spike that grips fur and clothes.
    Burr
    A hooked seed case that clings to whatever brushes past.
    Float
    To rest on water without sinking.
    Explode
    To burst open suddenly, throwing seeds out.
    Pod
    A long seed case, like the one peas grow in.
    Droppings
    Animal poo — a surprising free taxi for seeds.

    Try it yourself: collect 5 different seeds outdoors (or from fruit at home). For each, guess its travel style: wind, water, animal-fur, animal-food or explosion? What clue gave it away — wings, fluff, hooks, floatiness or a tasty package?

    Glossary

    Germinate
    To start growing from a seed.
    Seed coat
    The protective outer skin of a seed.
    Embryo
    The tiny baby plant inside a seed.
    Food store
    The packed lunch inside a seed that feeds the embryo.
    Warmth
    Gentle heat that tells seeds it is safe to grow.
    Oxygen
    The gas in air that living things need.
    Sprout
    To send out the first root or shoot.
    Soil
    The top layer of earth where plants grow.
    Swell
    To grow bigger by taking in water.
    Conditions
    The surroundings a seed needs before it will grow.

    Try it yourself: the classic experiment — put bean seeds in 3 jars: (1) water + warmth, (2) water + fridge, (3) dry + warmth. Check daily for a week. Which jar sprouts? What does that prove seeds need?

    • Sound zooms through water about four times faster than through air — about 1,500 metres every second!Source: NOAA Ocean Service ↗
    • Space is totally silent — there is no air to vibrate, so sound cannot travel there at all.Source: Adler Planetarium ↗

    Glossary

    Sound
    What we hear when vibrations reach our ears.
    Vibration
    A fast back-and-forth movement.
    Wave
    The moving pattern that carries sound through a material.
    Source
    The vibrating object where a sound starts.
    Travel
    To move from one place to another.
    Medium
    The material sound moves through.
    Vacuum
    Empty space with no air or other material.
    Eardrum
    The thin skin inside the ear that vibrates with sound.
    Vocal cords
    The folds in your throat that vibrate when you speak.
    Ear
    The body part that collects and hears sound.

    Try it yourself: stretch a rubber band between two fingers and pluck it. Watch it blur, hear it hum, then pinch it still — the sound stops instantly! Try the same with a ruler over a table edge. What stops the sound each time?

    Did you know?

    • Listening to sounds louder than 85 decibels for a long time can slowly damage your hearing.Source: NIDCD (NIH) ↗
    • The loudest animal on Earth is the sperm whale — its clicks reach about 230 decibels, louder than a jet engine!Source: Britannica ↗

    Decibels around you

    Rustling leaves ~20 dB

    About as quiet as a whisper in the library

    Talking ~60 dB

    Normal conversation level — comfortable for ears

    City traffic ~85 dB

    The warning line — long exposure starts harming hearing

    Thunder ~120 dB

    Close thunder hurts — cover your ears!

    Ear defenders

    Builders and ground crew wear them where decibels soar

    Glossary

    Volume
    How loud or quiet a sound is.
    Loud
    Having a big, strong sound.
    Quiet
    Having a small, soft sound.
    Decibel
    The unit used to measure how loud a sound is.
    Amplitude
    The size of a vibration or wave.
    Sound meter
    A device that measures volume in decibels.
    Noise
    Unwanted or unpleasant sound.
    Hearing
    The sense that lets you notice sound.
    Whisper
    To speak extremely softly.
    Roar
    A very loud, deep sound.

    Try it yourself: borrow a free sound-meter app with an adult. Measure: your bedroom at night, normal talking, the TV, the street. Rank them in decibels. Does anything at home pass 85 dB — the hearing-safety line?

    Did you know?

    • Bats hunt using squeaks with frequencies up to 212,000 hertz — far too high for human ears!Source: Britannica ↗
    • Most people can only hear sounds between about 16 hertz and 20,000 hertz.Source: Britannica Kids ↗

    Pitch around you

    Morning birdsong

    Small birds, fast vibrations — the highest natural sounds around

    Thunder rumble

    Huge slow air vibrations — nature's lowest notes

    Voices

    Children's vocal cords are shorter — that's why kids' voices are higher

    Piano keys

    Left end: long slow strings, low notes. Right end: short fast strings, high notes

    Ambulance sirens

    Sirens sweep from low to high pitch so everyone notices

    Glossary

    Pitch
    How high or low a sound is.
    High
    A sound made by fast vibrations, like a whistle.
    Low
    A sound made by slow vibrations, like a big drum.
    Frequency
    The number of vibrations per second.
    Hertz
    The unit of frequency: one vibration per second.
    Fast
    Moving many times each second.
    Slow
    Moving few times each second.
    Squeak
    A very short, very high sound.
    Rumble
    A long, deep, low sound.
    Note
    A musical sound with one particular pitch.

    Try it yourself: line up 4 glasses with different amounts of water and tap them with a spoon. Which glass sings highest — the fullest or the emptiest? Order them from lowest to highest pitch, then check with a tuner app!

    Did you know?

    • A whisper is only about 15–20 decibels, but a roaring jet engine is around 150 decibels.Source: Ducksters ↗
    • The bigger the vibration, the louder the sound — that is why hitting a drum harder makes more noise.Source: Science Learning Hub NZ ↗

    Changing volume around you

    The volume knob

    It tells the speaker cone to vibrate bigger or smaller

    Cheerleaders' megaphones

    A cone aims all the voice energy at the crowd

    Curtains and carpets

    Soft furnishings absorb echo and calm noisy rooms

    Earmuffs at fireworks

    Little ears wear protection at loud festivals

    Piano pedals

    The soft pedal makes hammers strike more gently

    Glossary

    Force
    A push or hit that starts a vibration.
    Harder
    With more force.
    Softer
    With less force.
    Energy
    The power stored in a movement or sound.
    Muffle
    To make a sound quieter by covering its source.
    Absorb
    To soak up sound energy instead of reflecting it.
    Insulation
    Material that blocks sound from passing through.
    Distance
    How far you are from the sound source.
    Megaphone
    A cone that aims sound in one direction.
    Earmuffs
    Padded ear covers that block loud sound.

    Try it yourself: put a ticking phone-alarm in an open bowl and listen from across the room. Now wrap it in a towel, then in a box with a blanket. How many layers until you cannot hear it? Which material muffled best?

    Did you know?

    • Blue whales sing super-low songs that other whales can hear up to 1,600 kilometres away.Source: NOAA Fisheries ↗
    • Orchestras tune to a note called A that vibrates exactly 440 times every second (440 Hz).Source: Britannica Kids ↗

    Changing pitch around you

    Guitar frets

    Each fret shortens the string — every step is a higher note

    Filling a bottle

    The glug-glug rises in pitch as the air column shrinks

    Flutes and recorders

    Covering holes lengthens the air column for lower notes

    Your own voice

    Muscles tighten your vocal cords to sing higher

    Tuning pegs

    Twist to tighten = higher; loosen = lower

    Glossary

    String
    The stretched wire or cord that vibrates on an instrument.
    Length
    How long something is.
    Tight
    Stretched hard, with lots of tension.
    Loose
    Not stretched tightly.
    Thick
    Wide and heavy, not slim.
    Thin
    Slim and light.
    Air column
    The air inside a tube or bottle that vibrates to make sound.
    Shorten
    To make something shorter.
    Tune
    To adjust an instrument until each note is exactly right.
    Instrument
    A tool made for playing music.

    Try it yourself: stretch a rubber band over an open box. Pluck it, then (1) pull it tighter, (2) press a pencil partway along to shorten it, (3) try a fatter band. Which change makes the note higher? Which makes it lower?

    Did you know?

    • Scientists think much of the universe is made of mysterious dark matter that nobody can see!Source: Britannica Kids ↗
    • There are more than three states of matter — the Sun is made of a fourth state called plasma.Source: Science Sparks ↗

    Particles around you

    Smell of breakfast

    Food particles fly through the air to your nose — gas in action

    Ice cubes

    Rigid shape = particles locked in a neat grid

    Juice takes cup shape

    Liquid particles slide over each other into any shape

    Pumping bike tyres

    You squash gas particles closer — compression!

    Balloons

    Gas fills every corner of the balloon evenly

    Glossary

    Matter
    Anything that takes up space and has mass.
    Particle
    A tiny piece of matter, far too small to see.
    Solid
    Matter with a fixed shape, like ice or wood.
    Liquid
    Matter that flows and fills the bottom of its container.
    Gas
    Matter whose particles fly freely and fill any space.
    Flow
    To move along smoothly, like water in a river.
    Container
    Anything that holds matter — a cup, a bottle, a room.
    Compress
    To squeeze something into a smaller space.
    Spread
    To move outward in every direction.
    Model
    A simple scientific picture that explains how something works.

    Try it yourself: ask an adult to spray a little perfume in one corner of the room while you stand in the far corner. Time how long the smell takes to reach you. What does this tell you about how gas particles move?

    Did you know?

    • Water boils at 100°C at sea level, but on a high mountain it boils at a lower temperature — so cooking an egg takes longer!Source: USGS Water Science School ↗
    • When water freezes it becomes about 9% less dense — that is why ice cubes float in your drink.Source: USGS Water Science School ↗

    Water's key temperatures around you

    Freezer at −18°C

    Well below 0°C — water there can only be ice

    Cooking phở broth

    Bubbling hard means the broth has hit ~100°C

    Body temperature 37°C

    Between water's two key points — our bodies are mostly liquid water

    Sa Pa frost

    On rare 0°C nights, northern Vietnam's puddles turn to ice

    Ice floating in drinks

    Solid water floats on liquid water — very unusual for matter!

    Glossary

    Temperature
    How hot or cold something is.
    Thermometer
    A tool that measures temperature.
    Celsius
    The temperature scale where water freezes at 0°.
    Melt
    To change from solid to liquid.
    Melting point
    The temperature at which a solid turns liquid.
    Boil
    To bubble fiercely as liquid turns to gas.
    Boiling point
    The temperature at which a liquid boils into gas.
    Freeze
    To change from liquid to solid by cooling.
    Ice
    Water in its solid state.
    Steam
    Water in its gas state.

    Try it yourself (with an adult): put a cooking thermometer in a pot of heating water. Record the temperature every minute. What happens to the reading once the water starts boiling hard — does it keep climbing past 100°C?

    Did you know?

    • The water you drink today is the same water woolly mammoths drank — Earth has been recycling it for over 4 billion years!Source: National Geographic Kids ↗
    • The whole water cycle is powered by just two things: the Sun's energy and gravity.Source: USGS Water Science School ↗

    Drying laundry

    Sun and wind speed up evaporation from wet clothes

    Sweaty glass of iced tea

    Air vapour condenses on the cold glass — not a leak!

    Foggy bathroom mirror

    Hot shower vapour condenses on the cool mirror

    Morning dew

    Overnight cooling condenses vapour onto grass and spiderwebs

    Shrinking puddles

    After rain, watch puddles evaporate hour by hour

    Glossary

    Evaporation
    Liquid slowly turning into gas at the surface.
    Condensation
    Gas cooling back into liquid drops.
    Water vapour
    Water as an invisible gas in the air.
    Water cycle
    Water's endless journey between sea, sky and land.
    Cloud
    A floating crowd of tiny water droplets in the sky.
    Precipitation
    Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail.
    Puddle
    A small pool of rainwater on the ground.
    Dew
    Water drops that form on cool surfaces overnight.
    Surface
    The top or outside layer of something.
    Dry
    Having lost its water.

    Try it yourself: draw around a puddle with chalk after rain, then re-draw its edge every hour. Where did the water go? Now breathe on a cold mirror — where did that fog come from? You have just seen both halves of the water cycle!

    Did you know?

    • Water dissolves more substances than any other liquid on Earth — that is why it is called the universal solvent.Source: USGS Water Science School ↗
    • If you spread all the salt dissolved in the oceans over the land, it would form a layer as tall as a 40-storey building!Source: USGS Water Science School ↗

    Solutions around you

    Sweet iced tea

    Sugar (solute) + tea (solvent) = one delicious solution

    The salty sea

    Earth's biggest solution — rivers have dissolved rock salts into it for ages

    Fizzy drinks

    A gas (CO₂) dissolved in liquid — bubbles are it escaping!

    Oral rehydration drinks

    Salt and sugar dissolved in exact amounts help sick tummies

    Making nước mắm dips

    Sugar dissolves in lime juice and fish sauce — solution skills in the kitchen!

    Glossary

    Solution
    A liquid with something dissolved evenly all through it.
    Dissolve
    To mix into a liquid so completely that it seems to disappear.
    Solute
    The substance that gets dissolved.
    Solvent
    The liquid that does the dissolving.
    Mixture
    Two or more substances together that can be separated again.
    Soluble
    Able to dissolve in a liquid.
    Insoluble
    Unable to dissolve in a liquid.
    Stir
    To move a liquid round and round with a spoon.
    Filter
    To separate insoluble pieces from a liquid using fine holes.
    Transparent
    Clear enough to see through.

    Try it yourself: test 5 kitchen solids in glasses of water: sugar, salt, flour, rice, coffee powder. Stir each 20 times. Which dissolve (transparent solution) and which just make a cloudy mixture or sink? Make a soluble/insoluble table!

    Did you know?

    • Your whole digestive tract is a tube about nine metres long — taller than five grown-ups standing on each other's shoulders!Source: National Geographic Kids ↗
    • Your salivary glands make about 1.5 litres of saliva every single day.Source: Science Kids ↗

    Your digestive system in action

    Mouth watering

    Smelling phở makes saliva flow — digestion prepares early!

    Different teeth, different jobs

    Front teeth slice; back molars grind like millstones

    Growling tummy

    That rumble is your stomach and intestines squeezing air about

    Upside-down swallowing

    Astronauts can swallow in space — muscles push food, not gravity

    A long journey

    A meal takes 1–3 DAYS to travel the whole nine metres

    Glossary

    Digestion
    Breaking food down so the body can use it.
    Mouth
    Where food enters and chewing begins.
    Teeth
    The hard cutters and grinders in your mouth.
    Tongue
    The muscle that tastes, mixes and pushes food.
    Saliva
    The mouth's liquid that softens food and starts digestion.
    Oesophagus
    The muscular tube from mouth to stomach.
    Stomach
    The stretchy bag that churns food with acid.
    Small intestine
    The long coiled tube that absorbs nutrients.
    Large intestine
    The wider tube that absorbs water from leftovers.
    Organ
    A body part with a special job, like the stomach.

    Try it yourself: chew a piece of plain bread for a full minute without swallowing. Notice it slowly turning SWEET — that is your saliva already breaking the bread down into sugars. Digestion starts in the mouth!

    Did you know?

    • The acid in your stomach is so strong it could dissolve an iron nail!Source: National Geographic Kids ↗
    • Wave-like squeezes called peristalsis push food along — you could even swallow while hanging upside down.Source: Science Kids ↗

    Digestion working for you

    Energy for playtime

    This morning's breakfast is powering your run right now

    Feeling full

    A stretched stomach signals the brain: enough for now!

    Germ defence

    Stomach acid destroys many germs hiding in food

    Blood delivery

    Nutrients ride the bloodstream to your toes and brain

    Growing taller

    Every centimetre you grow is built from digested nutrients

    Glossary

    Nutrient
    A useful substance from food that the body needs.
    Break down
    To split something big into tiny pieces.
    Churn
    To mix and squeeze over and over.
    Peristalsis
    Wave-like muscle squeezes that move food along.
    Enzyme
    A special substance that speeds up breaking food down.
    Acid
    The strong liquid in the stomach that dissolves food.
    Mucus
    The slippery coating that protects the stomach wall.
    Blood
    The body's delivery river for nutrients and oxygen.
    Waste
    The leftover parts of food the body cannot use.
    Fuel
    What the body burns for energy.

    Glossary

    Force
    A push or pull that can change how something moves.
    Push
    A force moving something away from you.
    Pull
    A force moving something towards you.
    Gravity
    The pulling force of the Earth on everything.
    Friction
    The force that slows things rubbing against each other.
    Air resistance
    Friction with the air that slows moving objects.
    Upthrust
    The upward push of water on floating things.
    Newton
    The unit for measuring force.
    Weight
    How hard gravity pulls on an object.
    Motion
    The movement of an object.

    Try it yourself: go on a 10-minute force hunt at home. Find one example each of: a push, a pull, gravity at work, helpful friction, and air resistance. Bonus: drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled one — which force makes them land differently?

    Did you know?

    • In a force diagram, a longer arrow means a bigger force — and the arrow always points the way the force acts.Source: Oak National Academy ↗
    • Forces are measured in newtons, named after the famous scientist Isaac Newton.Source: Britannica Kids ↗

    Glossary

    Diagram
    A drawing that shows forces as labelled arrows.
    Arrow
    The symbol used to draw a force.
    Direction
    The way a force pushes or pulls.
    Size
    How strong a force is, shown by arrow length.
    Label
    The name and value written beside an arrow.
    Act
    To work on an object, as a force does.
    Balanced
    Equal and opposite forces that cancel out.
    Unbalanced
    Forces that do not cancel, so motion changes.
    Resultant
    The single leftover force after combining all forces.
    Measure
    To find a value using an instrument.

    Try it yourself: pick 3 objects around you (a hanging picture, a floating toy in a basin, a book on the table). For each, draw the object as a box and add labelled force arrows. Are the forces balanced? How do you know from the object's motion?

    Glossary

    Earth
    The planet we live on.
    Sun
    The star that gives Earth light and heat.
    Year
    The time of one full orbit around the Sun: about 365 days.
    Rotation
    Spinning around an axis, like a top.
    Revolution
    One full journey of one object around another.
    Axis
    The imaginary line an object spins around.
    Spin

(Hint: how many days in a year?)

    Did you know?

    • When it is summer in Hanoi, it is winter in Australia — the two hemispheres always live in opposite seasons.Source: NASA Space Place ↗
    • Surprise: Earth is actually CLOSEST to the Sun in early January — during the northern winter! Distance does not cause the seasons; the tilt does.Source: NASA Space Place ↗

    Glossary

    Tilt
    A lean to one side instead of standing straight.
    Season
    One of the four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn, winter.
    Summer
    The warmest season, with the longest days.
    Winter
    The coldest season, with the shortest days.
    Spring
    The season when plants wake up and days lengthen.
    Autumn
    The season between summer and winter.
    Hemisphere
    One half of the Earth: northern or southern.
    Equator
    The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth.
    Sunlight
    Light that comes from the Sun.
    Temperature
    How hot or cold something is.

    Try it yourself: tilt-and-torch experiment! In a dark room, shine a torch straight at a wall — a small bright circle. Now tilt the torch: the same light spreads into a bigger, weaker oval. That is EXACTLY why the tilted-away hemisphere gets weak winter sunshine. Bonus: note down sunset time today, then again in a month — is daylight growing or shrinking?

    Did you know?

    • The Sun does not really rise or set at all — the Earth turns you towards it at dawn and away from it at dusk, at about 1,600 km/h at the equator!Source: NASA Space Place ↗
    • Sunrise and sunset skies glow red and orange because sunlight travels through extra-thick air near the horizon, which scatters away the blue light.Source: Britannica Kids ↗

    The Sun's daily schedule

    Ha Long sunrise

    Photographers face EAST over the sea to catch the rising sun

    Shadow clock

    Ancient people told time by the length of shadows

    Morning exercise

    Parks fill at dawn — cooler air before the Sun climbs high

    Fishermen's clock

    Boats head out before sunrise and read direction from the Sun

    Flag ceremony

    At Ba Đình Square the flag rises with the Sun every dawn

    Glossary

    Sunrise
    The moment the Sun appears in the morning.
    Sunset
    The moment the Sun disappears in the evening.
    East
    The direction where the Sun rises.
    West
    The direction where the Sun sets.
    Noon
    The middle of the day, around 12 o'clock.
    Shadow
    The dark shape made when something blocks light.
    Horizon
    The line where the sky seems to meet the ground or sea.
    Apparent
    Seeming to happen, though not real.
    Midday
    Another word for noon.
    Sky
    The space above the Earth that we see from the ground.

    Try it yourself: be a shadow scientist for one sunny day! In the morning, stand at the same spot and have someone mark the tip of your shadow with chalk. Repeat at noon and late afternoon. Compare: when was the shadow longest? Shortest? Which side did it point each time — and what does that tell you about where the Sun was?

    Did you know?

    • A camel's hump stores FAT, not water — a food supply that lets it march for two weeks across the desert without eating.Source: Britannica Kids ↗
    • A polar bear's fur looks white but is actually transparent — and beneath it, its skin is BLACK to soak up every ray of Arctic sunshine.Source: Nat Geo Kids ↗

    Rice plants thrive standing in water where other crops drown

    Sticky toe pads let house geckos sprint across the ceiling

    Wallowing keeps buffalo cool and blocks biting insects

    Migrating storks

    Flocks fly south each winter — an adaptation of behaviour

    Coconut palms

    Bendy trunks survive sea storms; floating nuts sail to new shores

    Glossary

    Adaptation
    A feature that helps a living thing survive in its home.
    Habitat
    The natural home of a plant or animal.
    Survive
    To stay alive despite difficulties.
    Environment
    Everything around a living thing: weather, land, water, other creatures.
    Desert
    A very dry place with little rain.
    Polar
    Belonging to the icy regions near the North or South Pole.
    Feature
    A part or quality that something has.
    Behaviour
    The way an animal acts.
    Blubber
    The fat layer that keeps sea animals warm.
    Gills
    The body parts fish use to breathe in water.

    Try it yourself: go on an adaptation hunt! Find 3 living things around your home (a pet, a bird, an insect, a plant on the balcony…). For each one, spot ONE feature and write what job it does: sharp claws for gripping? Waxy leaves for keeping water? Wings for escaping? Then the detective question: would this living thing survive in the DESERT? Why or why not?

    Did you know?

    • A cheetah sprints at over 100 km/h — but only for about 30 seconds, so a zigzagging gazelle that survives half a minute usually wins.Source: Nat Geo Kids ↗
    • An owl's eyes face FORWARD to judge striking distance; a pigeon's eyes sit on the SIDES of its head to watch for danger almost all around — hunter and hunted, written on their faces.Source: Britannica Kids ↗

    Hunters and hiders around you

    House cats

    Silent paws, night eyes, hooked claws — a living predator kit

    Stick insects

    Look exactly like twigs — champion hide-and-seek players

    Ambush hunters that drop their tails to escape being caught

    Bees and wasps

    Yellow-black stripes warn: I sting — leave me alone!

    Sparrow flocks

    Hundreds of eyes spot cats faster than one pair ever could

    Glossary

    Predator
    An animal that hunts other animals to eat.
    Prey
    An animal that is hunted by others.
    Camouflage
    Colours or patterns that help an animal blend in.
    Hunt
    To chase and catch animals for food.
    Escape
    To get away from danger.
    Claw
    A sharp curved nail on an animal's foot.
    Fang
    A long sharp tooth.
    Herd
    A large group of animals living together.
    Warning
    A signal that danger is near.
    Speed
    How fast something moves.

    Try it yourself: watch one hunt! Observe a house cat, a gecko near a lamp, or birds in the park for 10 minutes. Note down: what predator features do you see (eyes, claws, stalking moves)? What prey tricks do you see (freezing still, flying off together, watching in groups)? Who won, and which adaptation decided it?

    Backup to a file & restore

    Cách hoạt động · How it works

    Desktop Chrome/Edge: on the first Save, pick the folder containing this HTML file — every Save then writes the .json (named after this file + date-time) straight there, and each time the page opens it auto-loads the newest one (if the browser re-asks permission, tap the yellow bar). Phones/other browsers: the file downloads to Downloads; load it back with the yellow button.

    🌐 Get backup online (Google Drive or public GitHub)

    Thiết lập một lần (chỉ phụ huynh) · One-time setup (parent only)

    A public GitHub repo needs NOTHING extra — just paste the repo link (github.com/user/repo or …/tree/branch/folder). Google Drive only: browsers block webpages from reading Drive directly (CORS), so an API key is needed — create it free ONCE at console.cloud.google.com (project → enable the Google Drive API → Credentials → API key, with NO referrer restriction). It can only read public files. Share the Drive folder as "Anyone with the link — Viewer". Paste the key below — it is remembered and included in backups, so the child and other devices never need to touch this section.
